# Prediction, Generation, and Optimization {#sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization}

::: {.epigraph}
> "Data can tell you that the people who took a medicine recovered faster than those who did not take it, but they can't tell you why."
>
> — Judea Pearl and Dana Mackenzie, *The Book of Why* [@PearlMackenzie2018BookOfWhy]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *What job should AI perform, which method is suitable, and when is a conventional method or no AI better?*

**Core thesis:** *Choose a method by first naming the engineering role the work requires, such as proposing, screening, or searching, then the method family that can perform it (prediction, generation, or optimization), grounded in design-space structure, feedback cost, and comparison against strong conventional baselines.*
:::

When a parameter sweep is small enough to run directly and no qualified surrogate is already on hand, fitting and checking a learned model can cost more than completing the sweep itself. Direct simulation still requires a representative workload, a qualified simulator, and checks matched to the claimed result, and any learned method has to earn its place against that baseline by either reaching a comparable result at lower total cost or supporting a stronger architectural decision on the same budget.

That comparison points toward choosing the smallest method that solves the problem (@fig-ch05-cover-map). Prediction estimates design properties without running a full simulation, generation constructs register-transfer level (RTL) or configuration artifacts, and optimization steers search across large candidate spaces. What follows shows when each family fits, how to combine them, and when an analytical roofline model, an integer linear program, or direct simulation is the better choice. Once the time spent collecting data, fitting models, and checking outputs is counted, direct evaluation and conventional algorithms remain the baseline every learned method must beat.

![**The architecture problem dictates the smallest sufficient method.** In this schematic, four distinct conditions map to direct comparison, surrogate prediction, candidate generation, or closed-loop optimization. Each method pair couples an automated technique with a mandatory sanity check, a fallback to conventional tools, and an explicit stopping criterion to prevent unbudgeted search.](images/ch05-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch05-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which four architecture conditions map to direct comparison, prediction, generation, or optimization, with a named check, fallback, and stopping condition."}

## Engineering Roles and Method Families

Choosing a method gets easier once we separate the job a design system must do from the mechanism that performs it. Consider a small arithmetic datapath in our Lighthouse vision pipeline: to explore ways of implementing a required computation, an automated workflow has to construct a candidate datapath, estimate its area and delay, and decide which alternative is worth running through synthesis next. Construction, estimation, and selection are engineering roles; a method is a way of performing one or more of those roles by reading the design representation and returning an output that the next component or tool can use.

*Prediction* estimates a property or future state from the information supplied to it: for the datapath, a predictor might read the arithmetic graph, pipeline register locations, and target technology library to estimate area or critical-path delay before synthesis runs. Whereas an analytical model computes its estimate from explicit equations and hardware assumptions, a learned predictor fits those relationships from prior tool runs. In physical design, for example, PowerNet predicts dynamic IR drop,[^fn-ir-drop-c05] the local supply-voltage droop under switching current, from a design's power map before signoff analysis runs [@XieEtAl2020PowerNet]. Such predictions help rank alternatives quickly, though the estimate never substitutes for the signoff measurement used to check it.

[^fn-ir-drop-c05]: **IR drop**: A localized decrease in voltage within a chip's power distribution network caused by the resistance ($R$) of the wires and the current ($I$) drawn by switching transistors.

*Generation* builds the candidate artifact that a predictor or simulator will evaluate: for the datapath, a generator might rearrange the arithmetic operations and pipeline stages while preserving the required numerical behavior and interface timing, producing a concrete implementation to test rather than a score for an existing one. Generators can work from parameterized templates, compiler rewrite rules, or learned models, as when language models draft electronic design automation (EDA) tool scripts [@HeEtAl2024ChatEDA] and verification testbenches [@QiuEtAl2024AutoBench] or revise an RTL module after synthesis exposes a timing violation. Because the range of designs a generator can reach depends on the representation and rules it is given, every generated artifact still has to pass functional and physical checks.

*Optimization* chooses which candidate to evaluate next so that the search improves an objective within its constraints: for the datapath, an optimizer might seek lower energy per operation under fixed throughput, area, and clock-period limits. Rather than building an RTL block or predicting its delay directly, the optimizer uses the measurements or surrogate estimates gathered so far to spend the remaining evaluation budget well, as in black-box search over accelerator configurations [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo] or learned policies for cluster scheduling [@MaoEtAl2016DeepRM].

Naming these roles describes a design system far more clearly than naming its model architecture. In our datapath study, a generator can propose new pipeline organizations, a predictor can screen their area and delay, and an optimizer can decide which candidates warrant full synthesis, while functional tests check arithmetic equivalence and static timing analysis checks whether the circuit closes timing under the target library. Composed methods must agree on their inputs and outputs, but not every study needs all three families. A cache study comparing three capacity points can simply simulate all three, and an analytical roofline model[^fn-roofline-c05] can often expose the limiting bottleneck before any search begins. Knowing what each method family actually contributes is what lets an architect leave unneeded components out.

[^fn-roofline-c05]: **Analytical roofline model**: A visual and quantitative formulation that bounds theoretical peak compute performance and memory bandwidth to identify whether an operational kernel or pipeline is compute-bound or memory-bound [@Williams2009Roofline].

::: {.callout-war-story title="A method family carries its assumptions"}
**The claim.** Itanium's explicitly parallel instruction computing (EPIC) design moved instruction scheduling out of hardware into the compiler, assuming explicit parallelism, predication, and speculation would allow wide execution with static scheduling [@SchlanskerRau2000EPIC].

**The gap.** A static schedule cannot know every memory latency or control-flow outcome that will arise at runtime. EPIC therefore also provided speculation, predication, and mechanisms for handling variable latency [@SchlanskerRau2000EPIC]. Moving scheduling into the compiler changed how those uncertainties were managed; it did not remove them.

**The lesson.** A method family commits to its assumptions as firmly as to its mechanism. A method is viable only when its required information is available at the moment of execution.
:::

Within each method family, specific techniques differ in the representation they read, the data they require, and the cost and reliability of what they return. A linear regression fits weights over tabular features, whereas a graph neural network (GNN) passes messages along circuit connections; a large language model (LLM) predicts code tokens from context, whereas a constraint solver searches for assignments that satisfy explicit algebraic rules. The family names the broad operation, while the technique supplies the mechanism. Together with the engineering role and the way components are wired together, these choices separate design-system architecture into four distinct questions (@tbl-decision-layers).

| **Decision layer** | **Question** | **Choices** | **Required discipline** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Engineering role** | What work must be done? | Propose, screen, search, critique, repair, check, explain, coordinate. | Name input, expected output, limits, and next check for each role. |
| **Method family** | What broad operation performs the role? | Prediction, generation, optimization, or domain-specific operations. | Select operations from required outputs and feedback rather than fixed pipelines. |
| **Technique** | What concrete mechanism fits the artifact and feedback? | Conventional, learned, or hybrid techniques (analytical models, regression, Gaussian processes, GNNs, LLMs, Bayesian optimizers, solvers, heuristics). | State assumptions, applicable conditions, costs, and failure modes. |
| **System composition** | Which components must work together? | Single technique plus tools, or composed generators, predictors, optimizers, and retrieval modules. | Assign every component distinct inputs, outputs, costs, and checks. |
: **A design system connects engineering jobs to computational mechanisms.** Four decision layers separate roles, method families, concrete techniques, and system compositions. {#tbl-decision-layers tbl-colwidths="[18,22,34,26]"}

The system-composition layer becomes especially important when learned and symbolic techniques share a loop. A neural code model can draft an RTL edit, for instance, while a compiler or type checker rejects illegal syntax and port widths before simulation starts. In these neurosymbolic pipelines, learned components supply proposals or fast estimates, while symbolic components enforce explicit structural rules over compiler intermediate representations (IRs), abstract syntax trees (ASTs), or control-data flow graphs (CDFGs). What the pipeline actually guarantees depends on the exact rules the symbolic checker enforces, not on calling the combination "neurosymbolic."

An agent orchestrating such a pipeline still needs each component's inputs, legal actions, and outputs defined up front. Telling an agent to "improve the datapath" leaves open whether it should rewrite RTL, fit a surrogate, step a search algorithm, or run logic synthesis directly. Foundation models and retrieval modules can help an agent choose among those steps, but they do not replace the boundaries between the underlying tools and methods.

Whereas the four decision layers of @tbl-decision-layers describe how a method works internally, the three operational layers of @sec-three-operational-layers (@fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration) define how much of the hardware or software stack the workflow is permitted to change and which checks govern promotion.

Those two classifications cross rather than align (@fig-role-method-map). A Layer 2 closed-loop optimizer tuning macro placement inside a fixed floorplan uses prediction, optimization, or both without changing the chip's interfaces, whereas a Layer 3 co-design study might combine a generator that proposes new memory hierarchies with an optimizer that decides which candidate to simulate next. Because method choice and change authority are independent, combining a generator with a surrogate does not grant permission to alter a bus protocol, and exploring across hardware-software boundaries does not require using every method family. Regardless of which methods are composed, every candidate must pass verification matched to the claim being made, and any claim of physical readiness still rests on synthesis, place-and-route, and signoff tools rather than on the scope of the search.

![**Engineering tasks map dynamically across complementary method families.** In this schematic, starting from declared engineering roles (proposing, screening, searching, critiquing, repairing, checking, explaining, or coordinating), direct tool evaluation provides the default baseline. When an added method is justified, selection routes through prediction, generation, or optimization, executed via conventional, learned, or hybrid mechanisms that terminate in inspectable outputs and property-specific checks.](images/fig-role-method-map){#fig-role-method-map width="100%" fig-alt="Four-layer decision map. Eight engineering roles connect through a many-to-many relationship to prediction, generation, optimization, and another method family, with a direct-tool option. The technique panel groups representative concrete mechanisms as conventional, learned, or hybrid. Every path ends with an inspectable output and a named next check."}

Consequently, no engineering role is tied to a single method family: proposing candidates does not require a generative model, screening them does not require a neural network, and searching a parameter space does not require reinforcement learning. When an analytical bound or a direct simulator sweep already answers the question, the workflow can skip learned methods altogether; when an extra method is justified, the structure of the design artifact and its available feedback decide whether a conventional, learned, or hybrid technique fits best.

## Anchoring Architectural Method Selection

To decide whether an extra method is justified, an architect has to match what the method needs against what the design representation and tools can actually supply. A learned predictor needs representative training runs, a generator needs a representation that makes legal edits expressible, and an optimizer needs an objective and feedback signal that separate good designs from bad ones. Selecting a method begins with checking whether the study can meet those prerequisites and still come out ahead of a simpler baseline within its compute and engineering budget.

Start with what the study is allowed to change. In our arithmetic datapath example, choosing among three textbook adder topologies (ripple-carry, carry-select, and Kogge-Stone) is small enough that we can synthesize all three directly, whereas choosing where to place pipeline registers across an arbitrary network of arithmetic logic unit (ALU) stages opens a vast combinatorial space. When explicit algebraic constraints govern that space, an integer solver or domain heuristic often works best; when early choices restrict which downstream stages are legal, the method must track those sequential dependencies and filter out illegal configurations before launching multi-hour tool runs.

Next, ask what data is available to guide those choices, since the representations and datasets from @sec-data-representations-world-models limit which techniques can work in practice. A generator needs formal interface constraints and a representation it can edit cleanly, an optimizer needs consistent scores under a fixed objective, and a learned area or timing predictor needs prior runs from matching circuit structures and process corners. When matching synthesis runs are scarce, collecting training data and qualifying a neural surrogate will often burn more compute and calendar time than using an analytical model or running the candidates through synthesis directly.

Matching these requirements to the study's actual bottleneck shows where each method family earns its keep: generation helps when valid candidates are hard to write by hand, prediction helps when running the reference simulator or synthesis flow on every candidate is too slow, and optimization helps when the design space is too large to sweep exhaustively. Framing method selection around the bottleneck forces any added technique to prove its worth against a simpler baseline (@fig-method-selection-guide).

![**Method selection compares added capability with a credible simpler path.** In this schematic decision guide, the initial question is whether an added method could improve the supported result or lower total cost. If so, bottlenecks in construction, evaluation cost, or search-space scale suggest generation, prediction, optimization, or composed pipelines worth comparing; saturated verification paths suggest throttling arrivals or expanding checking capacity. Every branch terminates at declared support bounds, total cost accounting, property-specific checks, fallbacks, and stopping rules.](images/fig-method-selection-guide){#fig-method-selection-guide width="100%" fig-alt="Decision flowchart for method selection. An architecture decision and output lead to a test of whether an added method could improve the result or total cost. If not, retain the simpler conventional path. If so, limiting forms of work suggest methods worth comparing. Every branch ends at declared support, total cost, a named check, a fallback, and a stopping condition."}

The five branches in @fig-method-selection-guide map each bottleneck to a candidate response: drafting or rewriting missing artifacts (generation), screening out weak designs before expensive tool runs (prediction), steering search across large parameter spaces (optimization), planning multi-step edits whose effects depend on order (transition models), or pacing candidate admission when verification tools and licenses are already full. Even when a bottleneck points to a branch, the method still has to pay for itself. Slow synthesis makes a fast surrogate appealing only if its training cost and ranking accuracy leave a net savings in tool hours, just as a fast RTL generator wastes time if syntax errors and broken state machines flood the verification queue.

Practical operating constraints narrow the choice further. An interactive assistant that suggests RTL fixes while an engineer edits code needs sub-second latency, whereas strict rules around proprietary RTL, foundry process design kits (PDKs), or licensed timing reports may require every model to run on local machines. Error cost depends on how the output is used as well: a code suggestion that a human designer inspects before saving carries a very different risk from an automated netlist edit that feeds straight into place-and-route, and neither path becomes safe merely by swapping in a larger model.

Finally, every method must be paired with a check that can actually verify its claim. A clean compile cannot prove timing closure, a surrogate that ranks candidates well cannot prove that the winner meets a $3\ \text{W}$ power budget, and a testbench generated by the same model that wrote the RTL can easily share the same blind spot regarding corner-case protocol rules. Before spending the evaluation budget, the team should state where each method is trusted to work, what check qualifies its output, and what fallback takes over when those conditions fail (@tbl-method-role-limits).

| **Attribute** | **Question to answer before selecting the approach** |
| --- | --- |
| **Job and question** | What work should the method improve: constructing candidates, estimating consequences, selecting evaluations, or checking a property? |
| **Inputs and support** | Which represented state, artifacts, observations, workloads, design regions, and process assumptions may be used? |
| **Approach status** | Is the method active, candidate, conditional, or disqualified for this problem? |
| **Output and legal actions** | What exact output will be produced, and which legal actions or mutations are permitted? |
| **Evaluator and checks** | Which evaluator, simulator, model, or tool checks the output, and what property-specific check qualifies it? |
| **Feedback cost** | What are the compute, sample collection, training, and license costs of this method? |
| **Support and failure mode** | Under which conditions is the method reliable, and how will invalid outputs or unreliable estimates be detected? |
| **Fallback** | What simpler method or deterministic tool will be used if this approach fails? |
| **Stopping rule** | When does search or generation terminate: resolved decision, spent budget, or rejected slate? |
: **Method choice connects computational requirements to the conditions of a study.** The questions summarize the intended job, required information, outputs, checks, costs, and limits before the evaluation budget is spent. {#tbl-method-role-limits tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Select the Smallest Sufficient Method"}
**The principle:** Select the simplest method (whether conventional analysis, heuristic search, learned prediction, or candidate generation) that relieves the identified bottleneck.

**The application:** Use a conventional tool as the comparator when it meets the evidence requirement. Add complexity only when the expected improvement in result quality or total cost warrants qualification, integration, and checking; retain the simpler path when the added method does not earn that cost.
:::

Answering the questions in @tbl-method-role-limits requires looking closely at how each method family works in practice.[^fn-method-first-c05] We begin with prediction, asking what information a surrogate can use to estimate a design's behavior before the reference tools run.

[^fn-method-first-c05]: **The method-first anti-pattern in architectural research**: A recurring trap in academic ML-for-systems research where an investigation selects an advanced machine learning technique (such as deep reinforcement learning, graph neural networks, or generative diffusion) before identifying an actual engineering bottleneck. In contrast, rigorous architectural exploration practices bottleneck-first selection: verifying whether simpler closed-form analytical models, integer linear programming, or greedy heuristics already achieve the design goal at a fraction of the compute and maintenance cost.

## Predictive Surrogates and Reference Paths {#sec-prediction-estimating-behavior-before-full-evaluation}

A predictive surrogate estimates a quantity that would otherwise require a more expensive evaluation: for a floating-point fused multiply-add (FMA) unit in the Lighthouse vision pipeline, the surrogate might predict post-synthesis standard-cell area and critical-path delay directly from operation graphs before logic synthesis runs. Receiving a representation of a candidate and its relevant conditions, the surrogate returns an estimate that can help select candidates for evaluation so that a study examines a larger space with fewer detailed tool runs [@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE; @LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling]. The useful question is whether those estimates preserve the distinctions the design decision depends on.

Training such a surrogate requires pairing candidate inputs with ground-truth measurements from the reference flow: for our datapath area predictor, the inputs might be operator counts, bit widths, pipeline register counts, and target-library parameters, paired with cell-area reports from a fixed synthesis script. Fitting adjusts the model parameters on a training set, while held-out candidates test how well the surrogate generalizes to unseen designs. For the surrogate to save any time, every input feature it reads must be available *before* the expensive tool runs; feeding a post-synthesis predictor features that can only be extracted from a completed synthesis log defeats the purpose of screening. The representation choices from @sec-data-representations-world-models therefore dictate both what the predictor can see and where in the flow it can sit.

Within those representation limits, predictive techniques differ in the structural patterns they exploit and the volume of training data they require. They are practical alternatives matched to different problem shapes rather than steps toward a single all-purpose predictor: a simple closed-form equation or linear regression often suffices when a few dominant parameters govern the metric, whereas higher-capacity models earn their keep when nonlinear interactions across components drive the outcome (@tbl-prediction-techniques).

| **Predictive technique** | **Strong fit** | **Main reason to reject it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical / mechanistic cost model | Known relationships, limited data, inspectable assumptions. | Omitted interactions control the decision. |
| Linear / regularized regression | Stable tabular features, modest complexity. | Sharp response changes or uncaptured feature structure. |
| Decision trees / boosted forests | Tabular parameters, nonlinear interactions, mixed types. | Extrapolation into unobserved design regions. |
| Gaussian process | Costly evaluations, moderate dimensions, uncertainty coupling. | High dimensionality or dataset size making surrogate costly. |
| Neural network | Large datasets from matching conditions, complex nonlinearities. | Insufficient data coverage, latency limits, or confidentiality. |
| Sequence / transformer model | Programs, traces, reports, ordered context. | Token/sequence dataset size or deployment budget mismatch. |
| Graph neural network | Netlists, dependency graphs, circuit connectivity. | Node/edge features omit properties controlling the metric. |
| Analytical model + learned correction | Analytical model exists with repeatable residual error. | Correction data mismatch with current tool or workload. |
| Transition / world model | Actions alter subsequent states across multi-step planning. | Static scoring or direct tool feedback suffices. |
: **Predictive techniques differ in the structure and support they require.** Selection follows target consequences, data representations, available sample counts, and evaluation costs. {#tbl-prediction-techniques tbl-colwidths="[26,34,40]"}

The graph and sequence entries in @tbl-prediction-techniques show why matching the model to the circuit's structure matters. Two datapaths with identical adder and multiplier counts can wire those operators into very different critical paths, which a GNN can distinguish by passing messages along the dataflow graph rather than relying on flat summary counts. At the gate level, where each net connects a driver pin to multiple load pins as a directed hypergraph, connectivity and cell sizes give a graph model strong clues about logic delay; even so, wire capacitance and routing congestion depend on physical placement coordinates that a purely topological netlist graph does not contain unless layout estimates are supplied alongside it.

Time-varying circuit activity poses a similar representation test. A sequence model reading cycle-by-cycle toggle traces can separate bursty current spikes that look identical when averaged into a single activity factor. Turning those toggle sequences into accurate predictions of transient voltage droop, peak dynamic power, or glitch energy still requires timing windows and power-grid impedance parameters; a sequence architecture cannot recover physical context that was left out of its inputs.

Whereas all the predictors above score a static design snapshot, the final row of @tbl-prediction-techniques predicts how a design state changes in response to an edit. That capability matters when an architect or search algorithm applies a sequence of transformations in which early choices reshape the options and costs of later steps.

> **Architecture world model.** A learned predictor of how represented design state, permitted actions, and operating conditions affect subsequent state or measured behavior [@HaSchmidhuber2018WorldModels]. When it is scoped to how state or decision-relevant consequences change after an action sequence under stated conditions, it is a transition model. Either way it is a predictive technique rather than a universal design theory.

Sequential macro placement shows how a transition model works in practice: dropping a static random-access memory (SRAM) macro onto a canvas claims silicon area, blocks routing channels, and narrows where the next macro can legally sit. A learned transition model takes the current partial floorplan $s$ and a proposed macro placement action $a$ and predicts the updated floorplan state, $\hat{s}' = \hat{T}(s,a)$, allowing a planner to unroll short trajectories of candidate placements before invoking the physical router. This adapts the model-based planning formulation of @HaSchmidhuber2018WorldModels and @JannerEtAl2019MBPO to chip floorplanning, though those foundational ML studies do not themselves provide a qualified hardware placement model.

When a search loop uses such a world model, a planner compares short multi-step rollouts inside the surrogate, commits the best action to the real placement tool, and resets its starting state from the tool's returned floorplan while hard geometric checks enforce nonoverlapping macro boundaries at every step. Training a transition model requires logged step-by-step placement trajectories rather than just final wirelength scores on completed chips. Whether those rollouts pay off depends on whether the placement tool calls they save outweigh both the cost of collecting trajectory data and the compounding error of autoregressive steps; because small state-prediction errors accumulate over multi-step horizons, the planner has to re-anchor periodically against the actual EDA tool. Whenever direct evaluation is fast or a single-shot score is enough to rank candidates, a static cost predictor or direct tool call remains the simpler choice.

Whether a surrogate predicts a static metric or a multi-step state transition, its estimates mean nothing without a reference tool path to measure its error. In our datapath study, predicted cell area is checked against the post-synthesis area reported by the target EDA flow, while arithmetic correctness is verified separately by simulation or formal equivalence. Keeping the fast surrogate strictly separate from the reference tool path ensures that prediction error remains visible and that a model's estimate is never mistaken for a physical measurement (@fig-architecture-cost-model).

![**Predictions and reference-tool observations remain distinct.** In this schematic, a represented state and proposed action can be evaluated through a predictive model and through the tools chosen for the target property. Paired estimates and observations allow prediction error to be assessed under identified conditions. The reference may itself be a simulation or analytical model; its output establishes only the properties that configured path can evaluate.](images/fig-architecture-cost-model){#fig-architecture-cost-model width="100%" fig-alt="Diagram in which a represented state and proposed action feed a scoped consequence model and a separate tool path. The prediction and tool observation remain distinct and both enter a versioned study record."}

During initial model qualification, the workflow runs the same candidates through both paths in parallel, logging each surrogate estimate beside its reference measurement in the study record to measure residual error. Once active search begins, the surrogate filters the incoming stream of candidates and forwards only the top-ranked designs to the slower reference tools, while logging provenance, runtime, and pass/fail status for both paths. Running the reference tool on every candidate would erase the surrogate's speedup, but running the surrogate without periodic reference checks would leave model drift invisible when the search enters unfamiliar regions of the design space.

Even a well-tracked reference path only validates the specific physical or behavioral question that tool is built to answer. A surrogate trained on cycle counts from a microarchitectural simulator learns to imitate that simulator, not the gate-level timing or power of the final silicon. Architectural evaluation tools answer distinct questions rather than forming a single ranking of fidelity from rough to exact (@fig-eval-fidelity-latency): analytical models compute theoretical throughput and bandwidth bounds, SCALE-Sim and Timeloop estimate dataflow cycles and memory traffic for accelerators, gem5 simulates core and cache timing, Verilator checks cycle-accurate RTL behavior, FireSim runs field-programmable gate array (FPGA) simulations of full systems, and physical implementation flows measure timing slack, area, and power against a specific cell library.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-eval-fidelity-latency
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Architecture tools answer different questions rather than occupying one total ranking.** The schematic matrix maps six representative tool classes (vertical axis: Analytical / Roofline, SCALE-Sim / Timeloop, gem5, Verilator, FireSim, and Implementation / signoff flows) against six property domains (horizontal axis: Encoded bounds, Accelerator cycles and traffic, Microarchitectural timing, RTL behavior, Mapped execution, and Physical properties). A marked cell identifies a representative source of evidence under appropriate configuration. Empty cells omit other possible uses; they do not establish that a tool lacks every capability outside its marked domain. The actual evaluation path must record which properties its configured tools observe.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Matrix with tool classes as rows and property classes as columns. Marks associate analytical models with bounds, accelerator simulators with cycles and traffic, gem5 with microarchitectural timing, Verilator with RTL behavior, FireSim with mapped execution, and implementation and signoff flows with physical properties."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style
apply_style()
tools = ["Analytical / Roofline", "SCALE-Sim / Timeloop", "gem5", "Verilator", "FireSim", "Implementation / signoff"]
properties = ["Encoded\nbounds", "Accelerator\ncycles & traffic", "Microarchitectural\ntiming", "RTL\nbehavior", "Mapped\nexecution", "Physical\nproperties"]
coverage = {
    "Analytical / Roofline": [0],
    "SCALE-Sim / Timeloop": [1],
    "gem5": [2],
    "Verilator": [3],
    "FireSim": [3, 4],
    "Implementation / signoff": [5],
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.3))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.24, right=0.98, top=0.94, bottom=0.22)
for y, tool in enumerate(tools):
    for x in coverage[tool]:
        ax.scatter(x, y, s=95, color=COLORS["evidence"], edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.9, zorder=3)
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(properties) - 0.5)
ax.set_ylim(len(tools) - 0.5, -0.5)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(properties)))
ax.set_xticklabels(properties, fontsize=5.8)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(tools)))
ax.set_yticklabels(tools, fontsize=6.1)
ax.set_xlabel("Representative property focus", fontsize=6.5, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.45, zorder=0)
for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
plt.show()
```

Because each marked cell in @fig-eval-fidelity-latency reflects only what a given tool configuration observes, confirming a surrogate's IPC ranking in gem5 says nothing about whether the winning RTL will close timing at $3.0\ \text{GHz}$. A surrogate's training target, input features, and reference tool together define what its predictions can support; the next challenge is making sure those predictions stay reliable when an optimizer pushes the search toward the edges of the design space.

## Predictor Support Boundaries {#sec-support-limits}

A surrogate's measured accuracy holds only inside its *qualified support*: the range of circuit topologies, workloads, and process corners over which validation runs have shown its errors to be small. Stepping outside that support with a new datapath topology or technology node can break the model outright, but even inside the validated region, summary numbers like root-mean-square error (RMSE) or mean absolute error can hide mistakes that flip which design wins. A surrogate with low average error across thousands of random designs can still misclassify the handful of candidates sitting right against a hard area or timing limit.

Coupling the predictor to an optimizer makes that vulnerability systematically worse, because the optimizer actively seeks out candidates with the best predicted scores and therefore favors designs where the surrogate erred in a flattering direction. When tuning a vector lane or arithmetic pipeline, minimizing predicted energy steers the search toward designs where a coarse power model underestimated switching activity, just as maximizing predicted throughput favors designs where the model overestimated pipeline utilization. This selection bias, known as the *optimizer's curse* [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse], arises even when each individual prediction is statistically unbiased and every candidate stays inside the training domain.

Unmodeled physical effects can compound that statistical bias. Suppose a cycle-level core study uses an instructions-per-cycle (IPC) surrogate that ranks a 512-entry reorder buffer (ROB) with 16-wide issue at the top of the slate. If the simulator assumes a fixed clock frequency and ignores wakeup-cam capacitance and bypass-network wire delay, the winning configuration will likely fail static timing analysis at the target $3.0\ \text{GHz}$ clock, because wakeup and bypass delays grow with issue width and window size [@PalacharlaEtAl1997ComplexityEffective]. High simulated IPC means little if the circuit must slow its clock to function, so the reference check has to measure the cycle-time paths that the proxy left out.

We can see why selection bias occurs even without omitted physics by looking at $K$ fixed candidates whose estimates have zero-mean noise, $\hat{f}(x_i) = f(x_i) + \epsilon_i$. The expected value of the highest predicted score is always at least as large as the true maximum:

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i=1,\dots,K} \hat{f}(x_i)\right] \ge \max_{i=1,\dots,K} f(x_i).
$${#eq-optimizers-curse-bias}

Because maximizing over a slate picks up positive estimation errors (and minimizing picks up negative ones), unbiased point estimates still produce an optimistically biased winner (@eq-optimizers-curse-bias). Catching that optimism requires logging the surrogate's pre-selection prediction alongside the subsequent reference-tool measurement for every finalist, so that the team can compare predicted gain against confirmed gain without refitting the model in between and erasing the discrepancy.

When prior runs provide a reliable model of prediction noise, *shrinkage* can temper extreme estimates by pulling outlier scores back toward a prior mean in proportion to their uncertainty [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. In an architecture search, a team can estimate how much predicted speedup or energy reduction typically survives synthesis by saving prediction-confirmation pairs from earlier batches, fitting a shrinkage factor on data kept separate from the current finalists, and checking that the damped scores improve selection under the same rule. Because a single failed finalist is too little data to fit a correction factor, and because damping a noisy IPC score cannot supply a missing timing check, shrinkage works alongside reference tool verification rather than replacing it.

Keeping the optimizer's curse distinct from proxy gaming clarifies which fix applies where. The optimizer's curse comes from selecting the extremum of noisy estimates and happens even when the surrogate models the exact right objective. Proxy gaming, the architectural form of Goodhart's law [@Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement], happens when the objective itself omits a binding physical limit, such as optimizing IPC while ignoring clock period, and will mislead the search even if every IPC prediction is exact to the cycle. Shrinkage and out-of-sample confirmation address noisy estimates; only running a reference tool that measures the missing physical constraint addresses an incomplete proxy (@sec-law-optimizers-curse in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).

Because average error hides both failure modes near the frontier, a surrogate should be qualified using the metric that matches how the workflow actually uses its output. When the surrogate ranks candidates to pick a small batch for synthesis, rank correlation ($r_s$) measures global ordering agreement, while top-$k$ recall measures how many of the true best $k$ designs survive inside the model's top-$k$ slate.[^fn-ml-top-k-recall-c05] A model with high overall rank correlation can still drop the three best designs if its errors cluster near the Pareto frontier, whereas a model used to filter against a hard power or timing limit cares most about accuracy right around that threshold. Qualification therefore has to test the exact screening or selection rule that will govern the search.

[^fn-ml-top-k-recall-c05]: **Top-k recall**: The fraction of the measured best $k$ candidates that also appear in the predictor's top $k$. Ansor uses top-k recall, alongside pairwise comparison accuracy, to evaluate how well cost models rank tensor programs [@ZhengEtAl2020Ansor].

To test that screening rule directly, the workflow can run dedicated test batches from the intended candidate stream through both the surrogate and the reference tool. If the filter is discarding good designs, the team has to widen the survivor set, revise the rule, or pause screening while the cause is investigated, even though running those audit batches spends part of the tool budget the surrogate was meant to save. Auditing is especially important because an optimizer gradually shifts the candidate distribution away from the initial training set, degrading both point accuracy and uncertainty calibration over time [@OvadiaEtAl2019UncertaintyShift], and in multi-step transition models those errors compound further as each predicted state feeds the next step of the rollout.

When a candidate's point estimate lands close to a hard constraint, such as a predicted macro area of $1.42\ \text{mm}^2$ against a $1.50\ \text{mm}^2$ floorplan limit, or when a learned predictor provides no calibrated variance estimate, wrapping the prediction in an uncertainty interval gives the screening rule a clear margin for escalation. If the interval straddles the $1.50\ \text{mm}^2$ limit, the surrogate cannot settle whether the macro fits, and the candidate must be routed to the reference synthesis or placement flow. Split-conformal prediction[^fn-split-conformal-c05] builds such an interval directly from empirical errors on a held-out calibration set without assuming a parametric noise family [@LeiEtAl2018Conformal; @AngelopoulosBates2021Conformal]. Once we freeze the trained predictor $\hat{f}$, we evaluate it on $n$ calibration designs, compare each estimate against its reference measurement $y_i$, and retain the absolute residual $|y_i-\hat{f}(x_i)|$. Taking a high quantile of those calibration residuals supplies a common error margin $q_{1-\alpha}$ around each new prediction:

$$
\hat{C}(x) = [\hat{f}(x) - q_{1-\alpha}, \, \hat{f}(x) + q_{1-\alpha}].
$$

With $n$ calibration examples and a target coverage of $1-\alpha$, we set $q_{1-\alpha}$ to the $\lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil$th smallest residual (for instance, with $n=99$ calibration designs and a 90% coverage target where $\alpha=0.10$, $q_{0.90}$ is the 90th ordered error); if that rank exceeds $n$, the conservative margin is infinite. This finite-sample rank correction accounts for the calibration set size, and its coverage guarantee rests on *exchangeability*: the calibration examples and the next test candidate must be statistically interchangeable, so their ordering carries no information about their joint distribution. Under that assumption, a new reference observation falls inside its interval with probability at least $1-\alpha$:

$$
\mathbb{P}\left(Y_{n+1} \in \hat{C}(X_{n+1})\right) \ge 1 - \alpha.
$$

In conformal prediction, *coverage* means the probability that the interval contains the reference value, so a wide interval can achieve high coverage while settling few design decisions. The evaluation-cost model in @sec-method-evaluation-costs uses a different quantity, *screening coverage* $f$, for the fraction of comparisons settled without a reference evaluation (@eq-screening-efficiency-bound).

[^fn-split-conformal-c05]: **Split-conformal prediction**: A separate calibration dataset supplies residuals used to construct prediction intervals. Exchangeability between calibration and test samples supports the stated marginal coverage; the guarantee does not apply automatically to an adaptively selected finalist.

Because the conformal guarantee is marginal, it applies on average to a new exchangeable draw rather than separately inside every design region or to whichever candidate an optimizer selects. Adaptive search can therefore break the guarantee as soon as it steers future candidates toward regions the surrogate scored favorably, well before any workload or process change. Once candidates drift away from the calibration conditions, the interval width stays fixed and gives no warning that coverage has dropped. Out-of-distribution tests can flag unfamiliar inputs, but a quiet detector cannot certify that exchangeability still holds.[^fn-ood-c05] Because active optimization tends to sample the extreme tails of the surrogate's prediction distribution, empirical coverage on the selected finalists can degrade even while uniform random test batches still show nominal coverage.[^fn-conformal-covariate-shift-c05] Interval-based screening therefore requires ongoing reference checks on the candidate stream where it is used.

[^fn-ood-c05]: **Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection**: Statistical tests or model scores flag inputs that differ from a reference distribution. Such detectors can support escalation, but their false alarms and missed shifts need evaluation; a lack of alarms does not establish that conformal coverage assumptions hold.

[^fn-conformal-covariate-shift-c05]: **Conformal prediction under distribution shift**: Standard split-conformal coverage assumes statistical exchangeability between calibration and evaluation candidates. In active design space exploration, optimizers deliberately push toward unsampled frontier regions or exploit surrogate error valleys. Weighted conformal prediction can preserve marginal coverage under covariate shift when the conditional distribution of the outcome given the input remains unchanged, the test draw is independent of the calibration data, and the test-to-calibration density ratio is known on overlapping support [@TibshiraniEtAl2019CovariateShift]. Estimating that ratio introduces another source of error. These conditions do not automatically hold for candidates chosen adaptively from the same data, so reweighting alone does not qualify an optimization loop.

A practical monitoring rule compares the fraction of reference observations falling outside their predicted intervals over an audit window of $M$ cases against a declared tolerance: $\frac{1}{M}\sum_{k=1}^M \mathbb{I}(y_k \notin \hat{C}(x_k)) > \alpha + \epsilon_{\text{tol}}$, where $\mathbb{I}$ is one when an observation falls outside its interval and zero otherwise. Both the window size and the tolerance must account for sampling variation across repeated checks, making a threshold crossing an operational trigger to step in rather than a formal statistical proof that coverage has shifted. Audits must also sample candidates that screening would otherwise discard, since checking only survivors hides false rejections that quietly throw away good designs. When the monitoring rule signals that screening has become unreliable, two actions follow:

- **Suspend screening and escalate:** Turn off surrogate filtering and send affected candidates to reference checks matched to the claimed property, at a rate the available evaluation capacity can support. A simulation ranking claim goes to its declared simulator comparison; a physical timing claim goes to a timing check.
- **Revise and requalify:** Retain the discrepant measurements to update the model, then qualify the revised predictor and its intervals on fresh held-out data from the intended candidate population before turning screening back on, since retraining alone does not establish that the calibration assumptions hold again.

Prediction earns its keep only while its estimates preserve the distinctions that drive architectural choices. Even a well-calibrated surrogate, however, can only score candidates that already exist; constructing those candidate designs in the first place is the job of generative methods.

## Synthesizing Candidate Architecture Artifacts

Generative methods produce the concrete artifacts that a predictor or simulator will examine. In an image-filtering accelerator for the Lighthouse pipeline, for example, the starting specification fixes the 2D convolution operator, the fixed-point numerical precision, the streaming Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) protocol, and the physical area budget. Starting from those requirements, a generator can draft an initial RTL implementation or revise an existing design after tool feedback exposes a bottleneck, provided its output has enough structure to enter the tool flow as executable code or a formal design representation.

When synthesis feedback flags a long arithmetic path, the generator can reorder the operations or insert a pipeline stage if the surrounding interface tolerates the extra cycle of latency. The revised RTL then goes back through functional simulation and synthesis checks; if the added registers push area or switching power past the budget, the next revision can try a different datapath arrangement while preserving the required rounding and overflow behavior. Tool feedback thus guides structural edits to the hardware rather than merely scoring a fixed pool of candidates.

What kinds of structural edits a generator can make depends on how it builds the artifact. A parameterized template fills in knobs inside a fixed module skeleton, whereas a compiler transformation rewrites an existing intermediate representation using algebraic or scheduling rules, as Halide does when it separates the algorithm from the schedule [@RaganKelleyEtAl2017HalideCACM]. Grammar-based generators expand legal production rules and constraint solvers search for variable assignments that satisfy explicit equations; because both approaches preserve known structural invariants by construction, they remain strong conventional baselines against which learned generators must be judged.

Learned generators replace those explicit rules with statistical models trained over code, graphs, or layouts. An autoregressive language model builds a file by predicting one token after another from the prompt and the tokens already emitted [@Chen2021Codex; @ThakurEtAl2023VeriGen]; although its internal step is next-token prediction, its engineering role is generation because its output is a complete program or RTL module. Graph generators instead emit nodes and edges directly, while spatial diffusion models form macro placements through iterative denoising, using guided sampling to steer cells toward wirelength or density targets [@LeeEtAl2025DiffusionPlacement]. Together, the design representation and the generative mechanism determine which hardware organizations the system can even express.

To adapt a learned generator to a specific chip project, a team can either retrieve relevant specifications and code examples into the prompt at inference time or fine-tune the model weights on internal design repositories. As ChipNeMo shows across its domain-adaptation and retrieval experiments for chip design [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo], neither path guarantees that a drafted module will obey the active specification, and both must respect the confidentiality and licensing limits that govern proprietary RTL and foundry process design kits (PDKs) (@sec-architecture-data-access; @tbl-generation-techniques).

| **Artifact or problem** | **Likely construction path** | **What the path can enforce or use** | **External check still required** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structured configuration / program | Template, grammar generator, solver, program synthesis. | Encoded syntax, types, and constraints. | Intended semantics and runtime behavior. |
| Software, script, or compiler code | Autoregressive model, LLM, constrained decoding. | Supplied context and schema restrictions. | Execution semantics and target behavior. |
| RTL | Autoregressive model / LLM evaluated with hardware benchmarks [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM]. | Supplied design context and grammar constraints. | Elaboration and structural checks; functional behavior, clock crossings, and reset behavior; post-synthesis logic equivalence checking (LEC); implementation timing, power, and physical feasibility. |
| Project-specific text or code | Retrieval-supported generation. | Retrieved documents and examples. | Source consistency and artifact-specific checks. |
| Netlist / connectivity object | Graph-generative / conditioned model. | Represented nodes, edges, graph constraints. | Electrical, functional, timing, and physical checks. |
| Placement or floorplan | Diffusion or spatial generator [@LeeEtAl2025DiffusionPlacement]. | Spatial distributions and boundary geometry. | Legalization, routing, timing, power, and design rule checking (DRC). |
| Mixed hard and learned constraints | Learned proposal plus solver, compiler, or repair step. | Hard constraints from solver; patterns from data. | Properties not established by encoded constraints. |
: **Generative techniques should match artifacts and available constraints.** Enforcing syntax during construction prunes invalid drafts but does not replace property-specific verification. {#tbl-generation-techniques tbl-colwidths="[22,26,28,24]"}

@tbl-generation-techniques separates the constraints a generator can enforce while drafting an artifact from the properties that external tools must verify afterward. Even when constrained decoding restricts a language model to a legal SystemVerilog grammar [@WillardLouf2023GuidedGeneration; @GengEtAl2023GrammarConstrained], a file that parses cleanly can still infer unintended latches, drive a net from two sources, omit reset logic, or violate clock-domain crossing rules. Hardware benchmarks such as VerilogEval and RTLLM go a step further by running generated modules against unit testbenches [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM], yet passing a benchmark testbench still falls well short of physical signoff.

The RTL row in @tbl-generation-techniques shows why physical signoff requires a full chain of downstream tools, each targeting a distinct class of failure. Elaboration and linting catch structural defects first, while simulation, clock-domain crossing (CDC) analysis, reset checks, and SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) under bounded model checking (BMC)[^fn-bmc-c05] test whether the state machine behaves as intended across a bounded cycle horizon. Passing those behavioral checks still leaves physical implementation open: a synthesis run in Yosys maps the RTL to a target standard-cell library, formal logic equivalence checking (LEC) verifies that synthesis preserved the golden RTL semantics, static timing analysis (STA)[^fn-sta-c05] in OpenSTA checks whether timing paths meet setup and hold targets, and power analysis evaluates switching and leakage against Unified Power Format (UPF) intent. Signoff depends on this entire chain of implementation evidence rather than on behavioral testbenches alone.

[^fn-bmc-c05]: **Bounded model checking (BMC)**: A formal verification technique that unrolls a sequential circuit for a fixed number of cycles ($k$) and uses SAT or SMT solvers to check whether an invariant property holds within that bounded execution horizon. A successful bounded check proves absence of bugs up to depth $k$, but does not by itself guarantee correctness across infinite execution lengths.

[^fn-sta-c05]: **Static timing analysis (STA)**: Graph-based analysis of circuit paths and modeled gate and wire delays against timing constraints (clock period, setup, and hold) without simulating dynamic input test patterns.

A design loop can catch many of those structural errors before launching slow EDA tools if it pairs learned proposals with fast symbolic checks: abstract syntax tree (AST) passes and static compiler analyses inspect program structure in milliseconds, while Boolean satisfiability (SAT) and satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers verify encoded algebraic constraints. Those same structural rules, however, also bound the set of designs the generator can reach. Because a grammar that locks in a three-stage pipeline cannot invent a five-stage organization no matter how many textually distinct files it writes, an architect should judge candidate diversity by hardware structure and cycle behavior rather than by surface differences in source code.

That scrutiny has to extend to generated testbenches and assertions as well. When the same model or prompt drafts both the RTL module and its unit test, a shared misreading of the specification will let a buggy design pass its own testbench undetected. Catching that common-mode error requires an independent reference model, separately derived formal properties, or a golden trace that was not produced by the same generator.

Even when an independent check confirms functional correctness, a generator that ignores physical budgets can still emit unusable hardware. In a high-level synthesis (HLS) pragma search, for instance, aggressive loop unrolling and array partitioning can exhaust field-programmable gate array (FPGA) block RAM or cause severe routing congestion even though the generated C++ code is completely legal. The generator therefore needs explicit resource ceilings during construction, and its output still has to pass downstream synthesis and place-and-route checks.

KernelBench[^fn-kernelbench-c05] shows just how steeply candidate survival drops across these stages when language models write CUDA kernels against PyTorch baselines [@OuyangEtAl2025KernelBench]. The raw number of drafted kernels tells us very little about useful engineering output, because most candidates fall out between compiling cleanly, passing numerical correctness tests, and actually beating the baseline runtime (@fig-ch05-kernel-funnel).

[^fn-kernelbench-c05]: **KernelBench evaluation framework**: An empirical benchmark evaluating machine-generated GPU kernels against specified PyTorch baselines across functional correctness, compilation validity, and wall-clock execution speedup on target accelerators (such as NVIDIA L40S or H100) [@OuyangEtAl2025KernelBench].

```{python}
#| echo: false

Blue bars show correctness; hatched green bars show kernels both correct and faster than PyTorch Eager. The dashed line marks all tasks. Values come from Tables 1, 9, and 10; Llama Level 1 correctness uses Table 9's 26%, while Table 10 prints 27% for that cell.

Every bar sits below the dashed line, and the fast share never exceeds the correct share; Llama-3.1-70B scores zero on both at levels two and three."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Source dataset: data/datasets/chapter5-kernelbench-funnel.csv
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]

with open(
    _root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter5-kernelbench-funnel.csv",
    encoding="utf-8",
) as fh:
    dataset_rows = list(csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")))

model_order = [
    "Llama-3.1-70B Instruct",
    "DeepSeek V3",
    "OpenAI o1",
    "DeepSeek R1",
]
models = ["Llama-3", "DS-V3", "OpenAI-o1", "DS-R1"]

def dataset_values(metric, level):
    selected = {
        row["model"]: float(row["value_pct"])
        for row in dataset_rows
        if row["metric"] == metric and row["kernelbench_level"] == str(level)
    }
    if set(selected) != set(model_order):
        raise ValueError(f"Incomplete KernelBench dataset for {metric}, level {level}")
    return [selected[model] for model in model_order]

correct = {
    level: dataset_values("correct_one_shot", level)
    for level in (1, 2, 3)
}
fast1 = {
    level: dataset_values("correct_and_faster_than_eager", level)
    for level in (1, 2, 3)
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(5.5, 2.05), sharey=True)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.09, right=0.985, top=0.78, bottom=0.22, wspace=0.10)

width = 0.36
xs = range(len(models))
for ax, level in zip(axes, (1, 2, 3)):
    ax.axhline(100, color=COLORS["muted"], linewidth=0.8, linestyle=(0, (4, 3)),
               zorder=1)
    ax.bar([x - width / 2 for x in xs], correct[level], width=width * 0.94,
           color=COLORS["blue"], zorder=2,
           label="correct" if level == 1 else None)
    ax.bar([x + width / 2 for x in xs], fast1[level], width=width * 0.94,
           color=COLORS["evidence"], edgecolor="white", hatch="////", linewidth=0,
           zorder=2,
           label="correct and faster\nthan baseline" if level == 1 else None)
    for x, c_val, f_val in zip(xs, correct[level], fast1[level]):

            if val == 0:
                ax.text(x + dx, 1.5, "0", ha="center", va="bottom",
                        fontsize=5.0, color=COLORS["muted"])
    ax.set_title(f"Level {level}", fontsize=6.6, pad=3)
    ax.set_xticks(list(xs))
    ax.set_xticklabels(models, fontsize=5.0)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 112)
    ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=6, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
    ax.grid(axis="y", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.55)
    for spine in ["top", "right"]:
        ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
    ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
axes[0].set_ylabel("share of tasks (%)", fontsize=6.4)
fig.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.54, 0.98), ncol=2,
           frameon=False, fontsize=6.0, handlelength=1.2, columnspacing=1.5)
plt.show()

correct_lo = min(min(v) for v in correct.values())
correct_hi = max(max(v) for v in correct.values())
fast_lo = min(min(v) for v in fast1.values())
fast_hi = max(max(v) for v in fast1.values())
```

Across the three difficulty levels, `{python} f"{correct_lo:.0f}"` to `{python} f"{correct_hi:.0f}"`% of one-shot kernels pass the correctness tests, whereas only `{python} f"{fast_lo:.0f}"` to `{python} f"{fast_hi:.0f}"`% are both numerically correct and faster than the PyTorch baseline. Although these one-shot figures reflect the models available in February 2025 and will shift as models improve, the gap between drafting code, passing tests, and speeding up execution is permanent. Even a high pass rate is only as trustworthy as the test harness that measures it: in the same month, Sakana AI reported that its AI CUDA Engineer, an evolutionary loop evaluated on KernelBench tasks, discovered a memory exploit in the evaluation script that let generated kernels bypass the correctness check, prompting the authors to harden the harness and revise their results [@SakanaAI2025AICUDAEngineer]. Whenever an automated loop optimizes directly against a test script, it will exploit gaps in the check just as readily as it improves the kernel.

Once the test harness is sound, an architect choosing a generator must weigh how accurately a model solves problems against how fast it emits tokens. A model with the highest accuracy on software benchmarks such as SWE-bench [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench] is often a slow, multi-step reasoning model rather than the fastest token generator, and neither benchmark score nor token throughput measures end-to-end turnaround once compiler runtimes, simulator queues, and multi-turn repair steps enter the loop.

Which property matters more depends on where the tool loop spends its time. When fast lint checks or interactive edits dominate turnaround, higher token throughput fits more revision cycles into a fixed wall-clock budget; when cycle-accurate simulation or RTL synthesis takes hours per run, shaving seconds off model inference barely moves total elapsed time, and a slower model that emits fewer broken drafts will finish ahead by sparing the downstream tools wasted runs. An architect therefore has to evaluate a generator by how quickly its proposals pass checks and converge inside the complete tool flow, rather than by isolated model benchmarks.

Because total loop cost includes every failed draft, compile step, and repair iteration, a study that reports only its single best generated artifact hides the work required to find it and leaves open whether a conventional autotuner could have reached a better design under the same budget. A fair comparison matches the input problem, downstream tool flow, and resource limits while varying only how candidates are constructed. @tbl-generation-construction-pair outlines a prospective HLS experiment built on this principle, separate from the published KernelBench study above.

| **Aspect** | **Prospective matched-construction comparison** |
| --- | --- |
| **Artifact and semantics** | Pin executable C/C++ compute kernel, target FPGA device and speed grade, clock, numerical tolerance, and Vitis HLS version before selecting constructors. |
| **Construction arms** | Predeclare strongest practical conventional HLS autotuner (Tcl pragma search or solver design-space exploration (DSE)) and one code-generating model. Both receive identical kernels and tool feedback. |
| **Shared tools and checks** | Both paths use the same Vitis HLS flow, C-simulation, C/RTL co-simulation, and Vivado synthesis, implementation, and timing checks for the target FPGA. |
| **Matched resources** | Pin context limits, wall-clock budgets, synthesis allowances, and expert setup allowances. |
| **Recorded result** | Retain attempted artifacts, synthesis failures, latency/initiation interval (II) metrics, resource utilization, tool costs, elapsed time, and expert hours. |
: **A generation comparison must match construction paths, rather than only final artifacts.** Matched conditions ensure conventional autotuners and generative models compete fairly. {#tbl-generation-construction-pair tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

When a generator runs inside a multi-turn loop, compiler errors and synthesis reports become feedback that steers the next edit, as Chip-Chat demonstrated when human engineers and language models iteratively revised Verilog for an 8-bit processor through to tapeout [@BlockloveEtAl2023ChipChat]. Verification can also move inside the construction step itself: a Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) over AST edits can run linters and unit assertions on partial syntax trees so that port-width or type mismatches are pruned before the model expands dependent modules. Deciding which partial tree to expand next turns candidate generation directly into a search problem.

Some workflows split this iterative loop across several language-model roles inspired by multi-agent debate [@DuEtAl2024MultiagentDebate], assigning separate prompts to draft RTL, inspect lint and CDC reports, write unit tests, and propose formal properties. Although dividing those roles clarifies the workflow structure, a second model's agreement is not an independent verification check: if the agents share the same ambiguous specification or model family, they can still ratify the same bug. True verification independence comes from separately derived formal properties, golden reference models, and deterministic EDA tools that can falsify a shared assumption.

**Generative failure modes: proxy-level rationales and unverified mechanisms.** That need for empirical falsification is especially clear when a language model accompanies its hardware proposals with plausible-sounding architectural explanations. Even when a generated configuration is legal, its natural-language rationale can fail in two distinct ways: it may optimize an intermediate proxy metric that actually worsens the overall decision score, or it may state a causal mechanism that a direct experiment refutes.

A small retained study illustrates both failure modes. Its preregistered protocol asked an LLM, in a single recorded call, to propose three legal systolic array geometries for a synthetic three-layer matrix-multiplication workload within a ceiling of 1,024 processing elements (PEs), while a fixed aspect-ratio heuristic received the same budget of four SCALE-Sim evaluations [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3]. The prompt defined the local decision score as $S = \text{total cycles}/\bar{U}_{\text{frac}}$, which divides SCALE-Sim's summed `Total Cycles` (excluding separately reported prefetch cycles) by the unweighted mean of per-layer utilization, $\bar{U}_{\text{frac}}$, as a compute-window metric rather than full workload latency. As a deliberate counterpoint, the model proposed a compact $32 \times 16$ array of 512 PEs on the hypothesis that a smaller rectangle would raise utilization on narrow layers. That candidate did achieve the highest utilization on the original workload (45.4% versus 41.2% for the $32 \times 32$ baseline), but cutting the PE count in half nearly doubled execution time from 13,917 cycles to 25,277 cycles, yielding a worse score of 55.6k against the baseline's 33.8k (@fig-ai-study-result a), a trade-off the model's own response noted as the candidate's likely failure mode. Because the objective function gave no credit for saving area, improving the intermediate utilization metric hurt the actual decision score.

The same experiment also exposed an unverified causal claim. When proposing its $16 \times 64$ array, the model argued that because the general matrix multiply (GEMM) layers were wider in $N$ than in $M$, a wide array would outperform a tall $64 \times 16$ array, and that transposing the workload ($M$ and $N$ swapped) would reverse the winner. Because the model stated an explicit falsifier, a separate mechanism probe outside both arms' evaluation budgets ran both geometries on the original and transposed workloads (@fig-ai-study-result b). On the original workload, the wide $16 \times 64$ array beat the tall $64 \times 16$ array as predicted (33.8k versus 55.0k), but transposing the matrices did not flip the ranking: $16 \times 64$ still won with 23.5k against 25.5k, refuting the directional hypothesis. Because the probe altered multiple workload dimensions at once rather than isolating array orientation alone, it disproved the model's stated explanation without establishing a replacement mechanism. Even the record of what the model was told carries a provenance limit: although the model's output and every simulator log remain intact, the prompt file stored with the study fails the cryptographic hash recorded before the call and omits how GEMM dimensions map onto array rows and columns, leaving open whether the prompt actually sent included that mapping.

(b) Paired-line plot of the mechanism probe with 16 by 64 outperforming 64 by 16 across original and transposed workloads, refuting the predicted reversal."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]

result = json.loads(result_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

arm_runs = [r for r in result["evaluations"] if r["arm"] in {"model", "conventional"}]

    "conventional_baseline_32x32": "H  32×32 baseline",

    "heuristic_64x16": "H  64×16",
}

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.6, 2.65), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.35, 1]})
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.22, right=0.985, top=0.82, bottom=0.22, wspace=0.42)
