On the primary comparison (@fig-ai-study-result a), the model's $16 \times 64$ proposal tied the $32 \times 32$ baseline to the cycle on the compute-window score (13,917 cycles excluding prefetch at 41.2% mean utilization, for a score of 33.8k), and the fixed heuristic reached the exact same best score within its four allotted runs. Because neither arm beat the baseline by the preregistered 1% margin, the study outcome is null, showing no advantage for the language model and leaving the $32 \times 32$ baseline in place. More broadly, a strong or tied evaluation score validates neither a performance gain nor the model's explanation for why the geometry worked: ranking candidates and testing causal mechanisms are distinct jobs, and an architectural study must verify causal claims with targeted diagnostic probes rather than trusting a generator's prose.

Templates, compilers, and learned generators give an architect ways to draft and revise candidate designs, while simulators, formal tools, and diagnostic probes test whether those drafts actually work. In most design spaces, however, a generator can emit legal candidates far faster than downstream tools can evaluate them, so the study needs an explicit search policy to decide which candidate earns the next simulator or synthesis run.

## Search Tactics and Budget Allocation {#sec-search-tactics-budget-allocation}

Deciding which candidate deserves the next tool run forces a trade-off between refining known good designs and testing unfamiliar regions of the space. When tuning an on-chip crossbar or memory interconnect, for instance, an architect can either adjust arbitration weights around a topology that already performs well under benchmark traffic (*exploitation*) or spend a simulation slot on a new buffer organization whose latency behavior is still uncertain (*exploration*). Because every cycle-accurate simulation or synthesis run consumes scarce compute and license time, each run spent probing an uncertain region is one fewer run available to polish a promising incumbent.

Surrogate-guided search formalizes this trade-off through an *acquisition function*, a scoring rule that combines a surrogate model's point prediction with its uncertainty to rank untested candidates. Whereas the predictor estimates what latency or power a candidate is likely to achieve, the acquisition function measures how valuable it would be to run the reference tool on that candidate next. Bayesian optimization alternates between these two components in a closed loop: it fits or updates the surrogate on completed runs, maximizes the acquisition function to pick the next candidate, runs the simulator or EDA tool, and folds the new measurement back into the model.

When maximizing a metric such as throughput, an upper-confidence-bound acquisition rule scores each candidate $x$ as $\mu(x)+\kappa\sigma(x)$, where $\mu(x)$ is the surrogate's predicted mean, $\sigma(x)$ is its predictive standard deviation, and $\kappa$ sets the weight on uncertainty. A high predicted mean pulls the search toward designs expected to perform well immediately, whereas a wide standard deviation makes an undersampled region worth testing even if its mean estimate is modest; when minimizing a cost such as energy or latency, the optimistic bonus simply subtracts $\kappa\sigma(x)$ instead. In either direction, a high acquisition score only marks a candidate as a priority to test next, not as a confirmed improvement or a feasible design.

How reliably that score guides the search depends on where $\mu(x)$ and $\sigma(x)$ come from. In a Gaussian-process surrogate, the observed tool runs determine both the posterior mean and the predictive variance through the chosen covariance kernel and noise model, cleanly separating the statistical model that estimates hardware behavior from the decision rule that picks the next experiment.

Other acquisition rules use that same predictive distribution to answer slightly different questions: expected improvement scores how much a candidate is likely to beat the best design seen so far, while information-gain criteria target points that will most reduce uncertainty across the Pareto frontier. Which rule fits best depends on whether the study needs to beat a known baseline in a few runs or map a broader trade-off surface, how much the next tool invocation costs, and whether the surrogate's uncertainty estimates remain valid in the region being searched (@sec-support-limits).

Whatever acquisition rule the optimizer uses, both the surrogate and the selector have to respect the discrete structure of hardware parameters. If a search treats cache set associativity in $\{2,4,8,16\}$ as an unconstrained continuous number, it will propose fractional ways that no simulator can run and measure distances between designs that make no physical sense; Gaussian processes with discrete kernels or input transformations, tree-based ensembles, and mixed-integer solvers preserve those valid choices by construction. Known architectural invariants should likewise be enforced before launching an expensive simulation, and any topology or instruction set architecture (ISA) change that lies outside the active parameterization requires expanding the representation before the search can explore it.

Running evaluations across a cluster of parallel simulator or EDA licenses changes how the acquisition rule dispatches candidates. A synchronous policy selects a diverse batch of candidates and waits for the entire batch to finish, whereas an asynchronous policy dispatches a new candidate as soon as a worker frees up. Under either scheme, the selector must account for the runs already in flight so that free workers do not pile onto the exact same point in the design space, unless the study deliberately repeats a run to measure simulator variance or verify a narrow margin. Batch and asynchronous scheduling thus trade the throughput of keeping every tool license busy against the better decisions that come from waiting for in-flight results to return.

When those tool runs return, the optimization loop must record failed and timed-out jobs for what they actually are rather than collapsing them into fake hardware numbers (@sec-data-representations-world-models). A simulation killed at a wall-clock cutoff provides only a right-censored lower bound on execution time [@KleinMoeschberger2003Survival], not a valid measurement of energy, area, or timing slack. Although an optimizer may train a separate classifier to predict timeout risk or attach an explicit penalty score to steer search away from failing regions, it must keep that steering penalty separate from genuine hardware measurements and distinguish design-induced failures from license drops or server crashes.

Beyond choosing which candidate to test next, multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization also chooses which tool fidelity to run [@KandasamyEtAl2017MultiFidelityBO]. A fast analytical model or short trace can screen out weak candidates cheaply when its rankings correlate with the reference simulator, even though it cannot verify physical properties it never models; the study must therefore log which tool produced every data point and hold back enough budget to confirm top candidates on the reference flow. Once a study has decided how to score candidates, schedule parallel runs, and mix tool fidelities, it still has to choose the concrete optimization algorithm that will step through the design space.

## Optimization Algorithms and Heuristics

The optimization algorithm that carries out the search has to match the mathematical structure of the candidate space. Different algorithms propose moves, incorporate feedback, and remember past evaluations in fundamentally different ways, and their relative performance shifts with the parameterization and experimental budget [@HendersonEtAl2018DeepRL; @KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. In spatial accelerator design, for example, stepping across discrete systolic-array dimensions poses a very different search problem from tuning continuous buffer partition ratios or placing macros on a non-convex floorplan, and those structural differences determine which algorithms are worth comparing.

At the simplest end of the spectrum, exhaustive enumeration evaluates every legal point in a small finite space, while uniform random search samples candidates independently to provide a transparent baseline. Domain heuristics build on human experience by encoding fixed engineering rules, such as resizing cells along a critical timing path first. Local search, simulated annealing, and evolutionary algorithms instead iteratively perturb existing candidates; in hardware design, their mutation and crossover operators must either preserve structural legality by construction or be followed by a repair pass, since randomly splicing two netlists or floorplans rarely yields a valid circuit. When each tool evaluation is too expensive for large populations, Bayesian optimization uses a surrogate's uncertainty to pick individual runs carefully, whereas differentiable optimization follows gradients across a continuous relaxation of the hardware and projects the result back onto discrete registers and gates, a rounding step that can easily erase the continuous gain.

When the objective and constraints can be written in closed algebraic form, mathematical programming and constraint solvers can search the discrete space directly without training a statistical policy, trading sample complexity for solver runtime. Equality saturation offers a related symbolic approach for datapath and compiler rewriting:[^fn-egraph-c05] whereas a greedy pass order can permanently overwrite an intermediate expression that would have unlocked a better downstream transformation, an equivalence graph (e-graph) applies rewrite rules monotonically to retain all equivalent forms at once until the graph saturates or hits a memory limit. An extraction pass then selects a low-cost netlist or schedule from the e-graph using dynamic programming or integer linear programming (as in the `egg` library), provided the rewrite rules are semantically sound and the workflow budgets for graph growth and extraction time.

[^fn-egraph-c05]: **E-graphs and equality saturation**: An e-graph (equivalence graph) compactly represents exponential numbers of equivalent algebraic or program expressions. Equality saturation applies rewrite rules monotonically while retaining earlier forms, reducing dependence on a greedy rewrite order. An extraction pass then selects a low-cost form among those represented, subject to the cost model, extraction algorithm, and search budget.

Before launching any of these optimizers across dozens of hardware knobs, an architect can also shrink the search space with a classical factor-screening experiment that estimates which parameters actually move the objective [@PlackettBurman1946Design]. Unlike surrogate candidate screening, which filters individual designs during a search, factor screening prunes unimportant knobs ahead of time. Its fractional-factorial estimates assume, however, that pairwise interactions do not mask the main effects: in a datapath where pipeline depth and operator sharing interact strongly, varying each knob in isolation can miss a combination that only works when both change together.

When design choices unfold sequentially and each step reshapes the legal options that remain, reinforcement learning (RL) can train a policy to pick actions from an observed state using cumulative rewards, though sequential structure alone does not make RL superior to classical tree search or analytical optimization. Macro placement is the most prominent hardware test case: because dropping a large SRAM or IP block onto a canvas alters the remaining whitespace and shifts wirelength and routing congestion for every subsequent block, an RL policy can place macros one by one while a terminal reward scores the completed floorplan (@fig-alphachip-placement) [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. Whether that learned policy beats mature classical placers remains contested: independent evaluations reported that analytical placement and simulated annealing matched or beat the RL results on tested benchmarks without pretraining a policy [@ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment], while the original authors disputed the 2023 comparison [@GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed] and the 2026 study evaluated updated code and pretrained checkpoints. Rather than settling a universal winner, the debate underscores that any learned policy must prove its net value against tuned conventional engines under matched compute and engineering budgets.

![**A placement policy learns to choose actions from a partial floorplan.** In this schematic of the reinforcement-learning macro placement framework [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement], the policy places macros sequentially, receiving an updated partial floorplan after each step. Once the macros are placed, an approximate standard-cell placement supports a proxy cost combining wirelength, congestion, and density; its negative supplies a terminal reward. Optimizing this reward still requires downstream checks of placement legality, routing, and timing, and rigorous comparison against classical analytical baselines [@ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement].](images/fig-alphachip-placement){#fig-alphachip-placement width="100%" fig-alt="Loop diagram with separate lanes for a placement policy's outbound macro-location action and the partial floorplan's inbound next state. After placing all macros, an approximate standard-cell placement precedes a density, congestion, and wirelength proxy cost, whose negative becomes the terminal reward."}

That compute budget has to account for the heavy upfront cost of policy training. Because running a full commercial place-and-route flow inside thousands of training episodes would exhaust both compute clusters and EDA licenses, the RL loop relies on a fast standard-cell proxy to estimate wirelength and congestion, deferring real routing and timing closure until the end. Placing dozens of macros before receiving a single terminal reward also complicates credit assignment, as the scalar score rarely reveals which early macro placement triggered a late routing bottleneck. For a learned placement policy to pay off, its final post-route signoff metrics must justify the upfront training runs; while fast proxy rewards and pretraining across chip blocks can help amortize that cost, transfer still has to be demonstrated on the actual target blocks.

When an architect is optimizing a single block or a one-off microarchitectural study with no opportunity to amortize pretraining across future chips, direct search, domain heuristics, or Bayesian optimization avoid that upfront training tax entirely. Under a fixed tool budget, the practical question is simply how much verified hardware improvement each method delivers before the budget runs out.

Which algorithm leads at the end of a run depends strongly on how large that evaluation budget is. A greedy heuristic or local hill-climber often improves rapidly on the first few evaluations and then stalls in a local trap, whereas Bayesian optimization or evolutionary search spends its early runs exploring the space before overtaking the greedy baseline later. In ArchGym's benchmark across architecture simulators, diverse search algorithms all reached the target specification once given ample samples and tuned hyperparameters [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym], showing that the differences that matter to architects appear under finite evaluation budgets. A fair comparison must therefore fix the tool budget and stopping rules in advance and charge every method for its full computational cost, including surrogate updates, policy training, and failed tool runs, rather than comparing only the final winning designs.

How the study formulates its objective shapes the search just as strongly as the evaluation budget. Minimizing datapath energy under hard area and timing ceilings is a constrained single-objective problem, whereas a team exploring trade-offs across power, performance, and area (PPA) can use multi-objective optimization to retain the set of nondominated designs, those for which no other evaluated candidate is at least as good on every metric and strictly better on at least one [@Deb2001MultiObjective]. Collapsing those metrics into a single weighted sum forces the architect to pick exchange rates before seeing what the hardware can do, whereas retaining the empirical Pareto front lets the team inspect the actual trade-off curve, bearing in mind that the retained points only approximate the true frontier over the candidates tested so far.

@tbl-optimization-methods summarizes where each search mechanism fits best, what structural assumptions it relies on, and how it typically fails. These entries offer a starting point for choosing baseline and experimental arms in a study, not rigid rules that validate or disqualify an algorithm by name alone.

| **Search procedure** | **Strong fit** | **Required conditions** | **Common mismatch** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Enumeration | Small, finite legal spaces where every candidate is evaluable. | Explicit action space, affordable exhaustive coverage. | Applying after space exceeds available budget. |
| Random search / sampling | Large spaces permitting independent samples; transparent baseline. | Legal sampler, matched budget, retained failures. | Treating as insurance against flawed objectives. |
| Deterministic heuristics | Spaces with exploitable domain structure. | Explicit rules, assumptions, clear stopping rules. | Hiding manual tuning or biasing search away from optimal regions. |
| Simulated annealing | Spaces with useful local moves and multiple local optima. | Legal neighborhood, acceptance and temperature schedules, evaluation budget. | Moves or cooling schedules that leave little opportunity to reach better regions. |
| Bayesian optimization | Costly evaluations where a surrogate can guide selection from limited observations. | Suitable representation, useful uncertainty estimates, acquisition rule, evaluation budget. | A surrogate or acquisition rule poorly matched to the candidate space or changing feedback. |
| Differentiable optimization | Continuous parameters or trustworthy relaxations. | Useful gradients, post-discretization verification. | Ignoring discretization gaps, yielding unrealizable hardware. |
| Evolutionary search | Discrete/mixed spaces with population variation operators. | Legal mutation/crossover or repair, sufficient evaluations for the population. | Too few evaluations to improve the population or weak comparison baselines. |
| Reinforcement learning | Sequential choices where learning a policy can repay its interaction cost. | Informative state, meaningful rewards, affordable training, demonstrated reuse when needed. | Paying to train a policy for a problem that direct search resolves more cheaply. |
| Mathematical programming / solvers | Algebraic objectives, discrete choices, explicit constraints. | Formalizable objectives and constraints. | Optimizing unrepresented architectural desiderata. |
: **Search mechanisms differ in the structure and feedback they require.** Suitability depends on the candidate representation, available evaluations, and cost of fitting or tuning the procedure. {#tbl-optimization-methods tbl-colwidths="[22,26,26,26]"}

When evaluating a learned optimizer selected from @tbl-optimization-methods, the first check is whether it beats simple baselines such as random search or basic domain heuristics on the exact same parameter space and tool budget [@BergstraBengio2012RandomSearch]. PrefixRL illustrates this discipline in prefix-adder synthesis by running commercial-grade logic synthesis directly inside its training loop and comparing the learned policy against classical adder topologies and synthesis scripts [@RoyEtAl2021PrefixRL].

Beating uniform random search is only a sanity check, however, because production synthesis passes, HLS autotuners, and physical-design engines already combine decades of domain heuristics with mathematical solvers. To show a genuine engineering gain, a study must benchmark its proposed optimizer against a well-tuned conventional tool flow under matched compute budgets (or document why no conventional baseline applies) and count setup, representation, and hyperparameter-tuning overhead alongside the final PPA improvement.

Just as the baselines must be fixed before the run starts, the stopping rules belong in the study protocol up front. A search loop can stop when a candidate meets its predeclared improvement and feasibility targets, when the run or wall-clock budget is exhausted (counting crashed and timed-out jobs against the budget they consumed), or when expected improvement drops below the cost of launching another batch. Meeting an acceptance threshold shows only that the design suffices for the engineering goal at hand, not that it is a global optimum; conversely, running out of budget without finding a legal candidate leaves open whether a larger budget or a wider parameterization would succeed.

Concrete stopping rules tie the optimizer to an architectural decision rather than an open-ended chase for a slightly higher score: a cache-capacity study can halt once a fixed run limit is reached or the candidate configurations are cleanly separated, while a datapath search can stop as soon as post-synthesis checks confirm a target energy reduction within area and timing budgets. Setting any of those run limits responsibly, however, requires calculating how many evaluations the available simulators, synthesis licenses, and screening stages can actually complete.

## Evaluation Capacity and Screening Cost {#sec-method-evaluation-costs}

A method must fit the evaluation resources available to the study. Two calculations establish that fit: how quickly the tool flow can process candidates, and how much reference evaluation a cheaper screen can reliably avoid. Both bounds apply whether candidates come from a conventional search, a learned generator, or a hybrid loop.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

### Quantifying Evaluation Capacity {#sec-sample-efficiency-under-expensive-feedback}

Every proposed candidate creates work for the tools that evaluate it. A generator can draft hardware blocks far faster than simulators and physical-design tools can measure them, and an optimizer can create the same mismatch by requesting runs faster than the tool flow completes them (@sec-evaluation-capacity-bounds-search). Setting a sustainable proposal rate therefore requires counting both how many evaluations each tool stage can finish and what fraction of proposed candidates survive early checks to reach it.

To keep slow simulators and implementation tools from becoming an immediate bottleneck, an evaluation path usually places fast checks ahead of expensive ones. Analytical rooflines test encoded throughput and bandwidth bounds, Spike checks functional execution, and gem5 models cycle-level contention, whereas physical-implementation questions require tools such as OpenSTA for static timing analysis (STA), power analysis under Unified Power Format (UPF) intent, and bounded model checking (BMC) over SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA).[^fn-eda-signoff-c05] Because each tool tests a different property, the evaluation path must match the architectural question: a fast functional check can filter out broken candidates early, but it cannot substitute for a slower timing or power check downstream.

[^fn-eda-signoff-c05]: **Signoff tools**: OpenSTA checks modeled circuit paths against declared timing constraints. UPF specifies power intent, such as voltage domains and power gating, for tools that analyze or verify it. SVA expresses properties; BMC checks them over a specified bounded execution horizon. In production physical signoff, these checks are coupled with physical design rule check (DRC) and layout versus schematic (LVS) verification using foundry rule decks in qualified tools, such as Siemens Calibre or Synopsys IC Validator. A commercial 3\ nm implementation claim therefore needs an applicable foundry-qualified signoff path. The Lighthouse cache plan has not established such a path; producing a layout in an academic flow would not supply it.

Even with early filtering, the candidate space can easily outstrip what the tool path can run. A single GPU operator's schedule space in AutoTVM can reach billions of implementations [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM], and the accelerator mapping spaces modeled with MAESTRO and Timeloop are likewise far too large to evaluate exhaustively [@KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO; @ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. Vast spaces like these require selective evaluation, yet even a small candidate set can exhaust the budget if each run takes hours or days of simulator and synthesis time.

To see how early pass rates and tool runtimes constrain the sustainable proposal rate $g$, we can model the evaluation path as a sequence of $M$ tool stages. For this baseline calculation, assume fixed mean runtimes and conditional pass rates, dedicated capacity at each stage, and no retries or returning candidates.[^fn-feedback-c05] Stage $i$ has $c_i$ parallel slots and mean runtime $t_i$, giving a service capacity $\mu_i = c_i/t_i$, while its conditional pass rate $p_i$ is the fraction of candidates tested at stage $i$ that advance to stage $i+1$.

[^fn-feedback-c05]: **Returning work in queueing models**: Retries and repeated evaluations add visits to tool stages. A model with returning work must include those visits in each stage's arrival rate; the one-pass product used here does not include them.

Because only candidates that clear all preceding stages reach stage $i$, its offered arrival rate is $\lambda_i = g \prod_{j=1}^{i-1}p_j$ (with the empty product at $i=1$ equal to one, since every proposal enters the first stage). Requiring incoming work to stay below available service capacity via the utilization ratio $\rho_i = \lambda_i/\mu_i < 1$ at every stage yields the queue stability bound in @eq-queue-stability-bound [@Kleinrock1975QueueingSystems]:

$$
g < \min_i \left( \frac{\mu_i}{\prod_{j=1}^{i-1} p_j} \right).
$${#eq-queue-stability-bound}

The minimum in @eq-queue-stability-bound identifies the bottleneck stage that saturates first as the proposal rate rises. Because the denominator $\prod_{j=1}^{i-1} p_j$ is the cumulative survival probability through stage $i-1$, improving a generator so that more of its RTL drafts pass early lint or compile checks *increases* that survival fraction and therefore *reduces* the maximum proposal rate $g$ that downstream simulation or synthesis stages can sustain. While spare downstream capacity lets those tools evaluate more promising designs, a stage that is already near capacity will instead accumulate a growing backlog unless proposal admissions are tightened or parallel tool slots are added. This inequality bounds steady-state flow rather than turnaround time: bursty arrivals and variable runtimes can cause queuing delays well below the bound, a short study may finish before a steady regime develops, and shared license pools or retries require additional accounting.

While every stage remains below capacity, the same conditional pass rates determine how many candidates clear the entire $M$-stage pipeline. Expected finalist throughput is:

$$
q = g \prod_{i=1}^M p_i.
$${#eq-finalist-throughput}

The final pass rate $p_M$ governs the finalist output rate in @eq-finalist-throughput, but it does not reduce the load entering stage $M$ itself, because every candidate reaching that stage consumes a tool run before passing or failing. Even after a finalist clears all $M$ modeled checks, selecting it for a design still requires comparing it against the baseline and running any remaining checks needed for the intended claim.

Putting @eq-queue-stability-bound to work in an actual study requires logging observed service times, conditional pass rates, parallel slot counts, failed runs, and repeat visits across the tool flow, while separating active execution time from time spent waiting in queues. When sustained arrivals threaten to exceed a stage's service capacity, an unbounded queue grows without limit, whereas a bounded execution harness must delay, block, or reject submissions by capping batch sizes, limiting in-flight evaluations, or applying token-bucket admission control. These rate limits act on tool requests rather than on a language model's token generation speed. The capacity bound also clarifies where methodological improvements can help: faster proposal generation is useful only when the evaluation path can absorb the extra traffic, whereas a saturated path needs fewer proposals, more tool capacity, or a reliable cheaper screen. That third option raises a separate question: how much expensive tool work can screening actually save?

### Screening Cost and Validated Coverage

A cheap screen reduces the load on an expensive reference evaluator only when it settles enough cases reliably. In on-chip SRAM or accelerator pipeline design, for instance, an early analytical area model might immediately rule out configurations that exceed maximum floorplan boundaries while sending any borderline candidate to a reference placement run. The net compute saving therefore depends on how often the screen can settle a comparison within the study's allowed error, and on what it costs to verify that the screening rule remains reliable.

In selective classification, a model trades the fraction of cases it answers against its error rate on those answers by abstaining on uncertain cases [@ElYanivWiener2010SelectiveClassification]. For architectural screening, *validated coverage* $f$ is the fraction of the target comparison stream that a qualified screening rule settles without calling the reference evaluation, under declared error limits. Validated coverage is not simply the rejection rate: an overly aggressive rule that discards useful designs along with poor ones may save tool time while defeating the purpose of the search.

To calculate the possible saving, count *service work*: the evaluation effort spent processing comparisons, excluding queue wait time. Let $c_{\mathrm{hi}}$ be the reference cost per comparison and $c_{\mathrm{cheap}}$ be the cost of a cheap check, measured in the same units (assuming here that screened-out cases and surviving cases share the same average reference cost; if their costs differ systematically, each group must be weighted by its own cost). Suppose a fraction $a$ of all comparisons receives a cheap check and a fraction $f \le a$ is settled there: because the unresolved fraction $a-f$ pays for both checks while the unscreened fraction $1-a$ goes directly to the reference path, a total share $1-f$ still incurs the full reference cost $c_{\mathrm{hi}}$. Screening adds $a c_{\mathrm{cheap}}$ per original comparison together with routing, qualification, auditing, and rework overhead, denoted by $\epsilon \ge 0$ after normalizing by $c_{\mathrm{hi}}$. Dividing the original reference cost by the resulting total cost gives:

$$
S_{\mathrm{screen}} = \frac{1}{(1-f) + a \cdot (c_{\mathrm{cheap}}/c_{\mathrm{hi}}) + \epsilon} \le \frac{1}{(1-f) + f \cdot (c_{\mathrm{cheap}}/c_{\mathrm{hi}}) + \epsilon}.
$${#eq-screening-efficiency-bound}

For fixed coverage and costs, @eq-screening-efficiency-bound reaches its upper bound only when every cheap check settles its case ($a=f$). Because a real workflow cannot know in advance which comparisons the screen will resolve, universal screening sets $a=1$ and pays the cheap-check cost on every comparison, including those that subsequently require the reference path. Even if the cheap check and its auditing overhead were completely free ($c_{\mathrm{cheap}} = 0$ and $\epsilon = 0$), the remaining fraction $1-f$ would still pay the full reference cost, capping the speedup at $1/(1-f)$ by the same unaffected-work argument as Amdahl's law [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. Conversely, when a screen settles too few cases or requires heavy auditing overhead, its total cost exceeds the reference work it avoids.

Comparing a structural legality check against a learned performance predictor shows why rejection rate and validated coverage differ. When an RTL draft violates a hard structural rule, rejecting it outright requires no simulation because the structural defect alone disqualifies it under the study's rules. When a predictor rejects a legal design because its estimated performance looks poor, however, the study needs empirical evidence that the screen is not discarding useful architectures.

To apply @eq-screening-efficiency-bound in a study, an architect must estimate coverage and screening error on a representative sample of the whole comparison stream. Auditing only the candidates that the screen passes or settles leaves performance on the omitted cases unknown and introduces selection bias [@Heckman1979SampleSelectionBias]. The study record should therefore report the sampling procedure, the uncertainty in the coverage estimate, and the decision-relevant error rate, especially false rejections of strong candidates. Because shared modeling assumptions can hide the same physical failure mode from both a cheap screen and a reference simulator, agreement between them validates the screen only up to what that reference path can check, and validated coverage must be re-verified whenever the candidate distribution or hardware–software stack shifts (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack).

Whereas the capacity model bounds how much candidate traffic each tool stage can serve, the screening model bounds how much reference evaluation work a cheap filter can avoid. Even when a screen cuts total service work, turning that reduction into shorter wall-clock turnaround still depends on queuing dynamics, parallel slot availability, and setup costs. Together, the two bounds determine whether combining multiple methods can save work or improve designs within the available budget.

## Composing Prediction, Generation, and Optimization {#sec-one-model-specialists-hybrid}

Every design search needs a source of candidates and feedback with which to compare them: generation can construct or revise candidates, prediction can estimate properties that are slow to measure directly, and optimization uses those estimates and measurements to choose the next step. Combining these method families is worthwhile when their interaction improves the study together, but it does not require every study to deploy all three.

Consider an illustrative redesign of the Lighthouse arithmetic datapath, sketched here as a prospective loop rather than a completed experiment. A generator proposes a new arithmetic organization or pipeline staging under the required computation and interface constraints. Once a candidate clears initial structural and functional checks, a qualified surrogate estimates its post-synthesis area and delay so that an optimizer can weigh those predictions against prior observations and the remaining budget before dispatching an expensive implementation run, whose returned energy, area, and timing measurements then guide the next selection or revision request.

How the loop responds to that measurement depends on which component the feedback implicates: a timing violation points back to a revised pipeline structure, whereas a large surrogate residual requires evaluating similar candidates directly or recalibrating the predictor before trusting its rankings again. Because newly generated datapath topologies can fall outside the predictor's training support even when they are functionally correct, all three components must share exact candidate identities and evaluation conditions while keeping surrogate estimates strictly distinct from tool-checked results.

These engineering roles need not correspond to separate models or execute once in a fixed order: while an evolutionary procedure can both construct variants and select among them, a neural generator can work alongside symbolic solvers or static compiler passes that enforce encoded constraints. AutoTVM and Ansor provide concrete examples of composing search with learned cost models for tensor programs [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM; @ZhengEtAl2020Ansor], although their pipelines serve those specific tensor-scheduling formulations rather than establishing a universal sequence for hardware design. As an exploration loop grows to include static analysis, repair, fault localization, and coordination, @tbl-method-role-handoffs specifies what each role produces and how the next role uses it, whether performed by a human architect, a conventional tool, or a learned component.

| **Engineering role** | **Concrete output** | **Next check or handoff** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Proposal** | Named candidate or experiment request with identified changes. | Verify legality and scope before invoking expensive tools. |
| **Screening** | Scoped estimate or ranking with predicted properties and uncertainty. | Route selected candidates to measurement path; retain predictions for qualification. |
| **Search** | Next candidate or experiment, selection basis, remaining budget. | Execute within the current search formulation; make any proposed change to that formulation explicit. |
| **Static Analysis** | Testable defect, missing assumption, or conflict tied to named artifact. | Use the finding to guide revision; check whether the revised candidate resolves it. |
| **Repair** | Revised artifact linked to parent and modification record. | Treat as fresh candidate; rerun affected checks. |
| **Checking** | Result from named check under declared conditions (including timeouts/failures). | Interpret what the check establishes and what remains untested (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). |
| **Diagnostic Localization** | Proposed mechanism and distinguishing contrast conditions. | Request targeted measurement; analysis does not substitute for verification. |
| **Coordination** | Ordered request graph with dependencies, budgets, and artifact IDs. | Hand requests to environment for tool orchestration. |
: **Each engineering role produces an output that another role can use.** Separating proposals, estimates, revisions, and checked results makes their different contributions explicit. {#tbl-method-role-handoffs tbl-colwidths="[20,38,42]"}

The repair and diagnostic rows in @tbl-method-role-handoffs show why these boundaries matter. A revised datapath is a new candidate: the earlier timing result belongs to its parent and cannot be carried forward as if no design change occurred. Likewise, a diagnostic localization proposes a mechanism to investigate, whereas only a targeted check tests whether that explanation holds. A single component can perform several roles, but its outputs must preserve these distinctions.

To decide how much of the datapath loop to build, we start by asking which engineering work is actually missing. When a few candidate implementations already exist and direct evaluation is affordable, neither generation nor a learned screen is necessary; when candidate construction is required but each design is cheap to evaluate, generation and optimization can rely directly on tool feedback. Only when individual evaluations are slow or expensive can a learned predictor make a comparable result cheaper or help find a better design within the same budget, provided its net benefit covers data collection, fitting, inference, qualification, and reference confirmation.

These choices lead to the compositions in @tbl-method-organization, which also notes where each typically sits across the three operational layers. Because a conventional baseline may already predict, construct candidates, or search using analytical models and heuristics, the table distinguishes the added method family from the underlying technique: "generation only," for example, means that generation is the only added family beyond the baseline, while compilation, checking, and reference evaluation remain mandatory across every row.

| **Composition** | **Typical operational layer** | **When justified** | **What must be established** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Direct tools / conventional technique | Conventional baseline | Analytical models, solvers, or direct simulations perform work economically. | Retain unless an added component improves result quality or total cost while preserving checks. |
| Generation only | Typically Layer 1 point assistance | New or revised artifacts are needed; direct checking is affordable. | Generated candidates meet the intended requirements at an acceptable construction and checking cost. |
| Prediction only | Any layer; screening within a study | Candidates require cheap screening before expensive simulation. | Achieve comparable results at lower total cost or better supported results at the same budget, including fitting, inference, qualification, and confirmation costs. |
| Optimization only | Typically Layer 2 parameter search | Selecting among existing candidates or legal actions requires a search. | Benchmark against simple baselines; stop when further search yields diminishing returns. |
| Generation + prediction | Layer 1 drafting with a screen | Candidate construction and cheap screening are useful before expensive evaluation. | Predictor has support for the generated structures; selected candidates receive the required confirmation. |
| Generation + optimization | Layer 2, or Layer 3 for coordinated revisions beyond the template | Candidate construction required under selective search budget without supported surrogate. | Optimizer uses direct tool feedback; generated candidates pass verification. |
| Prediction + optimization | Typically Layer 2 surrogate search | Surrogate enables selective search under expensive tool feedback. | Keep surrogate, acquisition rule, and confirmation stages separately inspectable. |
| Generation + prediction + optimization | Candidate for Layer 3; not required by it | Constructing alternatives, estimating consequences, and directing search each improve the study. | Their combined benefit exceeds fitting, integration, and checking costs at the required result quality. |
: **Pipeline components must earn their cost in the declared study.** Each composition addresses particular work and introduces qualification, integration, and checking costs. The layer column indicates typical placement, not a requirement; no composition confers a layer by itself. {#tbl-method-organization tbl-colwidths="[20,20,30,30]"}

As @tbl-method-organization shows, the generation-plus-optimization row fits a datapath search that constructs alternatives and evaluates them directly, whereas adding prediction is a separate decision justified only if the screen improves that search within the available budget. Even when a workflow combines all three method families, composing them does not by itself make the system AI-native unless it also revises candidate structures across abstraction boundaries with checks matched to the claimed result, including implementation and signoff evidence whenever physical readiness is claimed. The public study examined in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect carries generated designs through a physical-implementation flow, yet it neither establishes foundry signoff nor compares total cost against a matched conventional flow, leaving open whether such a pipeline reaches a comparable, physically realizable design at lower total cost. Comparing our compiler-tuning and cache studies shows how candidate space size and evaluation cost govern these choices in practice.

## Method Selection in Two Contrasting Studies

Two studies can both aim to select a better implementation and still need very different methods. Tuning a tensor operator can involve far more schedules than can be measured on the target hardware, whereas the prospective mobile system-on-chip (SoC) cache study compares only three capacities. Their contrast makes method selection concrete: how many alternatives need evaluation, where will useful observations come from, and what can the evaluation budget cover?

### Compiler Tuning versus Cache Evaluation

For a fixed tensor operator and hardware target, a schedule determines implementation choices such as loop order, tiling, and parallel execution. Because the space of legal schedules is vast, AutoTVM combines search over these choices with a learned cost model, running selected programs on the target hardware and using their measured runtimes to update the model [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. Compatible observations from earlier workloads can warm-start the model, but a preexisting dataset is not required because measurements accumulate during tuning.

Learning a cost model is attractive here because a relatively small sample of hardware timings can help prioritize millions of unmeasured schedules. Even so, that screening benefit must repay the measurements spent training the model as well as the overhead of fitting and inference: a large schedule space creates an opportunity for selective search, but it does not by itself prove that a learned model beats a conventional compiler heuristic or autotuner.

The illustrative Lighthouse cache study faces the opposite regime: it compares three discrete capacity settings (2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB) under a budget intended to cover direct static random-access memory (SRAM) screening and cycle-level simulation. Because no matching prior data exists, collecting simulator runs to train a surrogate would consume the same small evaluation budget needed to test the three candidates directly. Direct evaluation with analytical SRAM models and cycle-level simulation is therefore the proposed starting method (@tbl-worked-method-decisions), although execution remains pending until the models and simulator are configured.

| **Decision parameter** | **Tensor-program tuning plan** | **Illustrative cache study** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Job** | Select a schedule that improves operator runtime on the target hardware. | Compare 2\ MiB baseline against 3\ MiB and 4\ MiB without expanding scope. |
| **Inputs and support** | Fixed operator and target, legal schedules, compiler version, evaluation budget, measurements collected during tuning; compatible prior data if available. | Three proposed `l2.capacity` settings, hardware/software specifications, SRAM constraints, no prior matching data. |
| **Approach status** | Search and learned cost modeling, following the AutoTVM pattern; study-specific comparator and budget still required. | Analytical SRAM screening followed by matched cycle-level simulations of the supplied candidates; no added generator or learned surrogate. |
| **Output and legal actions** | Selected legal schedule with checked correctness and measured target runtime. | Modeled SRAM metrics and matched cycle-level simulation results for 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, or 4\ MiB only. |
| **Evaluator and checks** | Compile and check outputs against the operator specification; measure runtime under matched target conditions. | SRAM physical model checks limits; cycle-level simulation and power models return system metrics. |
| **Feedback cost** | Surrogate fitting, candidate compilation, target runs, tuning review. | Three SRAM evaluations, maximum four cycle-level runs. |
| **Fallback and stop** | Compare with an applicable default schedule or tuned operator implementation; set the measurement budget and stopping criteria. | If SRAM screening is unavailable, simulate performance while keeping physical feasibility unresolved. Stop at the declared decision or budget limit. |
: **Candidate space, available data, and feedback cost distinguish the method choices.** A large compiler schedule space can justify surrogate-guided search, whereas the proposed three-capacity cache comparison favors direct evaluation. The compiler plan draws on a published method; this comparison reports no new execution results. {#tbl-worked-method-decisions tbl-colwidths="[22,39,39]"}

The inputs and feedback-cost rows in @tbl-worked-method-decisions explain why the two studies diverge: whereas timings collected from a subset of schedules in the compiler study can guide selection across many remaining candidates, gathering training runs in the three-capacity cache study would already perform the comparison itself. Method selection follows how much useful search work remains after data collection. Although that balance would shift if the cache question expanded to many interacting parameters or if a qualified surrogate already existed, the three-capacity question requires only an explicit evaluation protocol specifying how the candidates will be compared and what the results can establish.

### Evaluation Protocol and Resource Budgeting

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="Lighthouse Cache Evaluation Plan"}
**Context.** The question is whether increasing cache capacity from 2\ MiB to 3\ MiB or 4\ MiB reduces frame time while meeting the subsystem's power limit and the cache's area and access-time limits.

**Application.** Evaluate the supplied capacities directly. First assess each cache organization with an analytical SRAM model, then compare candidates through matched cycle-level simulations. No learned surrogate is proposed for this small comparison.

**Outcome.** This is an evaluation plan, not an executed result. The physical models and simulator configuration still need to be established before the plan can determine feasibility or a preferred capacity.
:::

A sound evaluation plan must connect each capacity setting to the physical hardware it represents. Enlarging an L2 cache can reduce miss rates, but it also changes storage area, leakage power, and potentially access latency. Holding the workload and unrelated core parameters fixed keeps the comparison interpretable, whereas holding area, leakage, or access latency fixed across different capacities would hide part of the physical trade-off. Each capacity setting therefore requires a corresponding organization and a consistent rule for deriving its modeled properties.

The proposed limits in @tbl-lighthouse-approach-decision make that comparison concrete. Note that TSMC N3E is the stated implementation target rather than an available, validated technology model in this study; before relying on an SRAM estimate, the team must establish that the analytical model and its parameters support the target process and candidate organizations.

| **Plan detail** | **Lighthouse cache comparison** |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Selected approach** | Direct evaluation with no added learned components. |
| **Allowed change** | Vary only `l2.capacity` among 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB. Hold workload, software, and unrelated microarchitectural choices fixed; derive capacity-dependent organization and timing consistently. |
| **Required tool roles** | A suitable SRAM model estimates cache macro area, access time, and leakage for the target conditions. A configured gem5 simulation provides frame-time and miss-rate estimates; compatible power models estimate subsystem power. |
| **Evaluation budget** | Three SRAM evaluations and at most four cycle-level runs, including failed or repeated attempts. This is a proposed limit, not a demonstrated sufficient budget. |
| **Feasibility checks** | Check functional behavior and candidate identity. Require modeled subsystem power at or below $3\ \text{W}$, total cache macro area at or below $1.5\ \text{mm}^2$, and access time at or below $2.5\ \text{ns}$. Physical feasibility additionally requires implementation timing, power analysis (including declared power intent), and physical signoff checks (DRC and LVS) across characterized process corners. |
| **Performance comparison** | Compare frame time against the 2\ MiB baseline under matched conditions. Define how uncertainty will be assessed before execution; accept an improvement only when the resulting interval for baseline minus candidate frame time is positive. |
| **Fallback and stopping** | If SRAM screening is unavailable, simulation can still compare performance under explicit cache assumptions, but physical feasibility remains unresolved. Stop when the declared comparison is resolved or the budget is exhausted; report an inconclusive result if the available evidence does not separate the candidates. |
: **Direct evaluation gives the proposed cache comparison a concrete starting plan.** The small candidate set motivates the method choice, while the listed models, checks, and budget identify what must be established before a result can support that choice. {#tbl-lighthouse-approach-decision tbl-colwidths="[26,74]"}

The budget row in @tbl-lighthouse-approach-decision is tight: comparing three capacities within four runs leaves almost no room for tool failures, repeated baselines, or additional workload observations, and a run count alone does not establish the uncertainty of a frame-time difference. When the planned observations cannot separate a candidate's gain from comparison uncertainty, the study must report an inconclusive outcome or secure a revised budget rather than declaring the lowest observed frame time the winner simply because the budget ran out. Because this protocol evaluates supplied capacities along a fixed design path (@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales) rather than generating new cache organizations, its scope is matched directly to the question being asked.

Total engineering cost also extends well beyond the four simulation runs (@tbl-method-role-limits). Configuring gem5, establishing the cache and power models, securing tool licenses, and reviewing output logs all consume engineering effort before any learned component is added; @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces examines the physical definitions and tool interfaces needed to run such plans, while @sec-what-architect-owns explains why halting before dispatch preserves engineering integrity when those prerequisites remain incomplete. Because adding a surrogate would require data collection and qualification on top of that baseline setup, direct evaluation is the most economical choice for a three-candidate comparison, whereas in larger studies where prediction, generation, and optimization do belong together, deciding how to balance and calibrate them raises several open research problems.

## Open Questions

When architects combine prediction, generation, and optimization in larger design studies, five open research problems emerge:

- **When is it worth training a learned residual model on top of a fast analytical model, rather than simply running direct search?** Analytical rooflines and mechanistic area models capture first-order physical limits without needing any training runs, whereas a learned surrogate can pick up second-order layout congestion and contention effects that closed-form equations miss, much as hybrid solvers in fluid dynamics and weather forecasting pair a coarse physical conservation law with a learned correction. Training and qualifying that residual model, however, spends simulator and synthesis runs that could otherwise go directly toward evaluating candidate designs. We still lack practical ways to tell from a small pilot sample whether second-order physical effects are large enough to flip which design wins before we spend the budget to learn them, or to know how many tool runs a study needs before a hybrid residual model beats both pure analytical bounds and direct search.

- **How do we keep a surrogate's uncertainty estimates honest when an optimizer actively hunts for its highest predictions?** A surrogate with low average error on held-out test designs can still mislead an optimizer that systematically picks its most optimistic errors or pushes candidates outside the training distribution (@sec-support-limits). Offline reinforcement learning hits the same failure mode when a policy trained against a fixed reward model learns to exploit high-error regions unless held back by pessimistic uncertainty penalties. Because an active search violates the exchangeability assumption behind standard split-conformal intervals even inside familiar parameter ranges, while out-of-distribution detectors catch only unfamiliar inputs,[^fn-ood-c05] nominal error bars routinely fail on the exact finalists the optimizer promotes. We still need sequential calibration methods that correct for selection bias along a live search path, together with clear rules for when predicted gains have grown too small relative to model uncertainty and the search should switch back to direct simulation.

- **How can a generator propose genuinely new hardware organizations without flooding verification tools with broken designs?** Code-generation models and template engines often fall back on minor variations of familiar microarchitectures, even when the design representation allows completely different pipeline or datapath topologies. Building grammar rules, type checks, or equivalence-graph rewrites into the generator raises the share of drafts that compile, but clean syntax neither forces the model to explore new structures nor stops generated RTL from failing timing closure and routing downstream. An open problem is how to combine intermediate hardware representations with fast formal checks during generation so that a search can reach genuinely new, physically buildable Pareto trade-offs within a fixed verification budget, rather than simply turning out more defective RTL.

- **How should a search loop shift its evaluation budget as higher pass rates move the bottleneck downstream?** As the queue-stability bound (@eq-queue-stability-bound) shows, improving a generator so that more of its drafts pass early lint and compile checks sends a heavier stream of candidates into slow simulation and synthesis stages, which can quickly clog those tools if the proposal rate stays fixed. Tightening a cheap screen can protect the downstream queues, but qualifying and auditing that stricter screen consumes reference simulator and synthesis runs of its own. We still lack controllers that can dynamically split a fixed tool budget between generating new candidates, recalibrating cheap screens, and running full reference evaluations as pass rates change, keeping compute and tool licenses focused on whichever stage actually limits finalist throughput.

- **When a generator, a surrogate predictor, and an optimizer run together in a closed loop, how do we keep them from amplifying one another's blind spots?** Although @tbl-method-organization assigns clear roles to each component, linking them in a loop creates a new failure mode: the generator can propose novel circuit topologies that fall outside the surrogate's training support, and the optimizer can then chase the surrogate's wildest extrapolation errors. Tuning each component in isolation misses these cross-component failures, yet updating all three together can burn through the entire simulation budget on internal recalibration before finding a better chip. We still need principled ways to keep a generator within structural regions where the surrogate can quantify its uncertainty, and to tell ahead of time when a full three-part pipeline will actually beat simpler direct search once data collection, calibration, and repair costs are counted.

## Summary

Choosing a method begins with the engineering work the architecture question actually requires: whereas redesigning the Lighthouse arithmetic datapath may call for generating new implementations, estimating their physical costs, and searching across candidates, the three-capacity cache comparison can start with supplied candidates and direct evaluation. Because that contrast stems from the size of the candidate space, the prior data on hand, and the cost of each tool run, method selection is a concrete engineering calculation rather than a preference for a particular model family.

When a study does combine prediction, generation, and optimization, each family introduces assumptions that affect the others. A generated circuit structure may fall outside a predictor's supported range, an optimizer may favor a predictor's optimistic errors, and a higher early pass rate may flood the tools needed to evaluate surviving designs. A sound composition must manage these interactions explicitly and repay its setup, calibration, and auditing costs within the available budget.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Match the mechanism to the missing work.** Separate the engineering role, the method family, and the concrete technique. Choose among learned and conventional methods using the candidate representation, available data, feedback cost, and required verification checks.
- **Prediction guides evaluation within its supported range.** A surrogate can rank candidates or screen properties before expensive tool runs, but the optimizer's curse can still favor optimistic errors even among familiar designs. Qualify predictors for the exact selection decisions they drive, and confirm selected improvements on the reference evaluation.
- **Generation introduces new designs into the loop.** A generator can construct or revise a hardware organization rather than only tuning parameter values inside a fixed template. Its representation, construction rules, and sampling strategy determine which alternatives it reaches, while syntax, functional behavior, and physical implementation require distinct checks.
- **Optimization uses feedback to direct the search.** Search mechanisms differ in how they use problem structure, previous observations, and uncertainty. Match the mechanism to the legal actions and evaluation budget, account for downstream tool capacity and the cost and validated coverage of screening, and define stopping rules that permit an inconclusive result.
- **Compose methods only where their interaction pays for itself.** Prediction, generation, and optimization are complementary capabilities rather than mandatory stages or necessarily separate models, and combining all three does not by itself make a workflow AI-native. Compare any multi-component pipeline against a simpler baseline at matched total cost (including data collection, fitting, qualification, failed runs, and repair), and keep proposed candidates, predictions, and tool-checked results strictly distinct as feedback moves around the loop.
:::

A selected method still needs a reliable way to act on real engineering tools. Abstract candidate representations must become executable requests, evaluations must run under controlled conditions, and both measurements and tool failures must return to the search without losing their provenance. The execution environment that makes this discipline possible is the subject of @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces.
